r2.name: IDR outcome engine plus claim buying (No Surprises Act arbitration)
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (No Surprises Act, plus state surprise-billing IDR in states such as NY, TX, NJ)
r2.legal_basis: No Surprises Act, PHSA 2799A-1(c)(7) requires HHS/DOL/Treasury to publish IDR information: number of disputes, prevailing party, offers relative to QPA, IDRE, provider and payer identities and service codes. CMS releases these as Federal IDR Public Use Files (PUFs) every 6 months. IDR Operations final rule (June 2026) changes batching, fees and eligibility pre-checks, phased in through 2026-27.
r2.dataset: Federal IDR PUFs (CMS, semiannual, CSV/XLSX): dispute-level and line-item-level records with initiating party, provider/practice name, payer/TPA, CPT/service code, place of service, state, QPA, both final offers as a % of QPA, prevailing offer, IDRE entity, eligibility outcome and timing. Millions of line items since 2022, with outcome labels (winner and award). Pair with Transparency in Coverage MRFs for in-network rates.
r2.current_users: Heavily mined already. Provider side: HaloMD (dominant filer, lobbying, many payer lawsuits), Daffodil Health (AI-native IDR platform), Zotec Partners (publishes PUF analyses), Radiology Partners/TeamHealth/SCP/Envision in-house operations, Nutex Health. Payer side: Zelis, Claritev (ex-MultiPlan), 6 Degrees Health, Experian Health. Academics (Brookings, Georgetown CHIR) already model arbitrator variance. Payers are suing HaloMD and others over 'gaming' (Elevance and BCBS GA suits dismissed in 2026).
r2.ml_unlock: Per-claim win probability and expected award for each (code, payer, state, IDRE, offer) cell. With that model you can set the best final offer, decide which claims to file, and buy or advance on out-of-network claim receivables at a discount and arbitrate them yourself, like a litigation-finance or factoring book. A payer-side version would decide what to settle in open negotiation before IDR, since payers lose about 80-88% of decided disputes.
r2.path_to_1B: OON emergency, anesthesia, radiology and neonatology claims in dispute are worth several $B/yr. A balance-sheet model that buys claims at 30-50 cents and earns the arbitration spread could reach $100M+ in net revenue. But the field is crowded (HaloMD already holds this position at scale), political and regulatory risk is high (operations rule, possible QPA-anchoring legislation, payer litigation), and the market shrinks as these providers move in-network. Getting to $1B is credible only if the company becomes the out-of-network clearing house for both sides.
r2.why_now: PUF history now reaches 2022-2025. The 2026 operations rule resets the economics of batching and fees. Payers are pushing back hard. The arbitrage is probably near its peak, which argues against starting now.
r2.verified: Verified by search: CMS publishes IDR PUFs (CMS general-info doc; Zotec 2026 analysis of Q1-Q2 2025 PUFs); IDR Operations final rule finalized June 2026 (Sidley, Goodwin); HaloMD and Daffodil Health active with AI framing; payer suits against HaloMD dismissed 2026; Georgetown CHIR finds arbitrators differ significantly. From memory: provider win rates of about 80-88%, award multiples of QPA, exact PUF field list.

r2.name: Hospital and SNF distress underwriting from HCRIS cost reports (lend to or buy from at-risk providers)
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (Medicare)
r2.legal_basis: Medicare-certified hospitals, SNFs, home health agencies, hospices and FQHCs must file annual cost reports (42 CFR 413.20/413.24) as a condition of payment. CMS releases them publicly as HCRIS. Hospital price-transparency rule (45 CFR 180) and IRS Form 990 Schedule H (nonprofits) add more forced data.
r2.dataset: HCRIS (CMS, free bulk download, annual from 1996 on): about 6,000 hospitals, 15,000 SNFs and others, with balance sheet, income statement, payer mix, days, charges, uncompensated care, wage index and cost-to-charge ratios. Outcome labels can be joined from public records: closures and conversions (CMS POS file, Sheps Center rural closures), Chapter 11 filings, CHOW (ownership-change) files, Medicare terminations, SNF ownership and staffing (PBJ) data.
r2.current_users: Kaufman Hall/Vizient, Chartis (rural distress), Definitive Healthcare, Trilliant Health, Strata, Moody's/Fitch/S&P (muni hospital ratings), Sheps Center and academic distress models. ML underwriting of hospitals by a lender looks sparse; private credit and revenue-cycle lenders underwrite by hand.
r2.ml_unlock: A predictor of 12-36 month hospital and SNF distress, closure and ownership change, trained on decades of forced cost-report filings with closures and bankruptcies as labels. Use it to underwrite working-capital loans, receivables financing and sale-leasebacks to rural and safety-net hospitals and SNFs, or to price acquisitions and distressed provider credit.
r2.path_to_1B: About $300B+ of outstanding hospital and SNF debt, and provider M&A runs $10s of $B/yr. A specialty lender with a better default model can hold a $3-5B book at 10-14% yields, the fintech route to $1B. Risks: cost reports lag 1-2 years, rating agencies' models may be good enough, and lending is capital-heavy.
r2.why_now: Medicaid cuts under the 2025 reconciliation law, phasing in 2026-28, plus site-neutral pressure and the end of COVID relief create a wave of rural hospital and SNF distress while banks retreat. The gap between filing and distress is still mostly unmodeled outside rating agencies.
r2.verified: From memory only (HCRIS legal basis and contents, competitor list, debt figures); not searched because of the budget.

r2.name: MA risk-adjustment and RADV exposure scoring (insure or price plan clawback risk)
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (Medicare Advantage, Part C)
r2.legal_basis: 42 CFR 422.311 RADV audits. The 2023 RADV final rule allows extrapolation from PY2018 onward without an FFS adjuster, and CMS said in 2025 it would audit every MA contract each year. DOJ False Claims Act settlements and OIG coding audits are public. MA encounter data is available to researchers through ResDAC, not publicly.
r2.dataset: Public: RADV contract-level results as CMS releases them (sparse); CMS MA enrollment, risk scores and plan payment files by county and contract; Star ratings measure data; OIG contract-level audits of specific diagnosis-coding error rates (labels); DOJ settlements. Claim-level encounter data is restricted.
r2.current_users: Very crowded: Optum, Cotiviti, Episource, Reveleer, Datavant, Apixio, Edifecs, and many AI chart-review startups (Navina, Persivia, Vatica). Actuarial firms (Milliman, Wakely) model RADV exposure.
r2.ml_unlock: Contract-level prediction of RADV extrapolated clawback and FCA risk from public coding intensity (risk-score growth versus peers), OIG error-rate history and diagnosis mix. Could support RADV liability insurance, M&A diligence on value-based care groups, or shorting MA-heavy names.
r2.path_to_1B: RADV recoveries could reach billions per year once extrapolated audits run. Buyers are MA plans, value-based care groups and PE acquirers. But labels are few and coarse, claim-level data is not public, and incumbents dominate coding. This is unlikely to be a public-data moat.
r2.why_now: CMS's 2025 plan to audit every contract with extrapolation, the backlog of PY2018-2024 audits, and the v28 HCC model transition.
r2.verified: Search confirmed RADV extrapolation and PY2024 audit-method coverage (hccbuddy, Wolters Kluwer 2026). The settlements and competitor list are from memory.

r2.name: Medicare drug-negotiation selection and price forecasting (trade pharma or buy royalties)
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program)
r2.legal_basis: IRA Sec. 11001-11003 (SSA 1191-1198). CMS must publish the selected-drug list, the negotiated Maximum Fair Prices and explanations. Part D and Part B spending dashboards and the Part D Prescriber PUF are public.
r2.dataset: CMS Part D and Part B spending by drug (annual), Part D Prescriber PUF, MFP explanations (2026, 2027 and 2028 cycles), FDA Orange and Purple Books. Labels: actual selections and MFP discounts across 3 cycles (about 40 drugs).
r2.current_users: Sell-side equity research, specialized hedge funds, IQVIA, Avalere, ATI Advisory, PhRMA consultants. Selection forecasting is mostly deterministic and widely done.
r2.ml_unlock: Forecasting selection and the size of each drug's MFP haircut years ahead, which feeds pharma valuation, licensing and royalty pricing.
r2.path_to_1B: Value comes through trading or royalty purchase. Signals arbitrage away quickly and there are only about 15 labels a year. Poor fit.
r2.why_now: Part B drugs enter in the 2028 cycle; the 'pill penalty' fix debate continues.
r2.verified: From memory only.

r2.name: 340B duplicate-discount and diversion detection
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (HRSA 340B)
r2.legal_basis: PHSA Sec. 340B. HRSA OPAIS publicly lists covered entities, contract pharmacies and Medicaid billing designations. HRSA audit results with findings are posted publicly. The 2026 rebate-model pilot changes claims data flow.
r2.dataset: OPAIS registrations (tens of thousands of covered-entity sites and contract pharmacy relationships); HRSA audit results (several hundred per year, with diversion and duplicate-discount findings as labels); Part D PUF; state Medicaid files.
r2.current_users: Crowded: Kalderos (well funded, manufacturer side), Second Sight Solutions, Verity Solutions, Sentry, Macro Helix (McKesson), 340B ESP (BRG), Apexus.
r2.ml_unlock: Predicting which covered entities or contract pharmacies are likely producing duplicate discounts or diversion, for manufacturer recovery or rebate validation.
r2.path_to_1B: The program is $60B+ at WAC, but the buyers are a few dozen manufacturers. Kalderos holds the position and the policy is in flux. Weak for a new entrant.
r2.why_now: The HRSA rebate pilot started in 2026 and state contract-pharmacy laws keep changing.
r2.verified: From memory only.

r2.name: Underwriting and buying Brazilian court-ordered government debt (precatórios and pre-precatório claims against states and municipalities)
r2.jurisdiction: Brazil
r2.legal_basis: Constitution Art. 100 says government judgment debts are paid in a strict chronological order. CNJ Resolution 303/2019 makes courts publish the precatório lists, the payment order and the payments made. CNJ Resolution 331/2020 created DataJud, the national base of case metadata and procedural movements, and DataJud has a public API (verified). CPC Art. 189 and the public-hearing principle make case records public by default.
r2.dataset: DataJud public API. It covers procedural metadata and every movement (TPU-coded) for essentially every case in all 90+ courts, about 80M+ active cases, JSON over Elasticsearch, with a Python client (pydatajud). Each court also publishes its precatório chronological lists and payment reports as PDF/HTML. Combine these with state and municipal fiscal data from the Tesouro SICONFI and the Courts of Accounts. Labels: how long each claim took from filing to final judgment to listing to payment, how often rescissory actions or recalculations succeeded, and default or delay by debtor entity.
r2.current_users: Buyers include Precato (federal precatório anticipation), Ativos Precatórios (Recife; launched the 'Ativos Intelligence' AI tool in April 2026, about 1,000 intermediaries on its platform), plus funds and banks: BTG, XP and Jive/Mauá-type distressed funds, and FIDCs dedicated to precatórios. Legal-data vendors (Jusbrasil, Escavador, Digesto, Predictus) sell case lookup but do not take positions. Federal precatórios are already priced tightly. The fragmented, under-priced part is state and municipal paper and pre-final-judgment claims.
r2.ml_unlock: A model that prices each claim using the full movement history of millions of comparable cases. It would predict (a) the chance the claim survives appeals and rescission, (b) the final amount after recalculation, and (c) when the debtor will actually pay, from that entity's queue position, fiscal health and political payment behavior. The goal is to buy the long tail of small municipal and state claims and pre-precatório claims (still on appeal) at 40-70% discounts that no human desk can diligence economically.
r2.path_to_1B: The outstanding precatório stock is reported at about R$330B (Tupi/press 2025, unverified primary). The company would run as a balance-sheet originator: a FIDC or fund buys claims, the ML handles diligence and pricing, and securitized tranches are sold to institutions. Deploying R$5-10B at a 20%+ IRR spread gives a billion-dollar-plus asset manager/fintech. Risks: constitutional amendments repeatedly reschedule payments (EC 62, 94, 113/114; a 2025 PEC froze the market and cut prices), which is regime risk the model cannot learn, and incumbent funds are already active.
r2.why_now: Since DataJud's public API (2023-24), case movements for every court are machine-readable nationally for the first time. Before that, scraping 90 tribunals was the moat. After the STF struck down parts of EC 113/114 (2023), federal payment certainty rose, which pushes capital toward the riskier subnational paper where the edge is. LLMs can now read the unstructured decisions and calculation reports at scale.
r2.verified: Verified by search: DataJud public API exists (CNJ/Convergência Digital, pydatajud on PyPI). Ativos Precatórios launched an AI tool in April 2026 (fetched article). Press figure of a R$330B stock, and a 2025 PEC that froze the market and cut prices (Demarest PDF title). From memory: Res. 303/2019 and 331/2020 contents, the named competitors Precato/BTG/Jive, and discount ranges.

r2.name: Insurance for corporate mass-litigation liability in Brazil: judicial guarantee bonds and loss-portfolio transfers of labor and consumer claims
r2.jurisdiction: Brazil
r2.legal_basis: Same CNJ Res. 331/2020 DataJud regime and public case records. CPC Art. 835 §2 and CLT Art. 899 §11 let defendants replace cash judicial deposits with seguro garantia judicial (judicial guarantee insurance) or bank guarantees, which creates an insured risk that is decided in court.
r2.dataset: DataJud movements for every labor court (TRT/TST, about 3M+ new labor claims a year) and consumer case in the state courts (JEC), linked by CNPJ (company tax ID) to the defendant. Labels are the final outcomes: settlement or judgment, amount, time to resolution, and whether the guarantee was called. Together with company filings (CVM contingency notes), every large Brazilian company's litigation book can be reconstructed from outside.
r2.current_users: Litigation-management and analytics vendors: Jusbrasil, Predictus, Digesto, JUIT, Turivius, Projuris, Thomson Reuters Legal One, Deep Legal. Big banks and telcos run in-house contencioso de massa (mass-litigation) analytics. Surety insurers (Junto Seguros, Pottencial, Tokio Marine, Berkley) underwrite judicial bonds mostly on the defendant's balance-sheet credit, not case-level outcome models (memory, unverified). Nobody known prices and assumes whole portfolios of claims, the loss-portfolio-transfer/legacy model common for US/UK P&C.
r2.ml_unlock: Case-level and portfolio-level reserving: predict the payout distribution and timing of any company's open litigation book from millions of resolved comparable cases. Use it to (a) underwrite judicial guarantee bonds at better loss ratios, (b) buy a company's whole labor/consumer contingency book for a fixed fee (legacy run-off for litigation), freeing its balance sheet, and (c) run the claims with AI-driven settlement strategy.
r2.path_to_1B: Brazilian companies carry hundreds of billions of reais in disclosed litigation provisions and contingent liabilities (labor plus civil plus tax; memory, unverified). The judicial-guarantee surety line is among the largest surety lines in Brazil. As an MGA/insurer or run-off vehicle, the company earns underwriting spread plus investment float. Taking on even R$10-20B of liability portfolios supports a $1B+ specialty insurer, like legacy players Enstar/Catalina. Caveats: crowded analytics vendors, the regulatory capital needed (SUSEP), and labor-law reform risk.
r2.why_now: DataJud is the first national bulk outcome dataset joinable by CNPJ. Unstructured labor and consumer decisions are formulaic and LLM-readable. High Selic rates make it expensive for companies to tie up cash in judicial deposits, so demand for bonds and liability transfer is up.
r2.verified: Verified: DataJud public API. From memory: the CLT/CPC guarantee substitution rules, the competitor list, the surety market structure, and contingency magnitudes. I did not search whether any startup already does litigation loss-portfolio transfers in Brazil.

r2.name: Recovery pricing for Indian distressed credit (ARCs, NBFC collections, IBC claims) from eCourts, NJDG, DRT, NCLT and IBBI outcomes
r2.jurisdiction: India
r2.legal_basis: The eCourts Mission Mode Project (Phase III) and NJDG publish case status, orders and judgments for district and high courts. IBBI regulations require disclosure of CIRP outcomes (claims admitted versus realized, haircuts). DRT/DRAT and NCLT orders are public under the open-court principle. The SARFAESI and IBC statutory processes generate dated, labeled recovery events.
r2.dataset: eCourts services hold about 200M+ case records and orders (CNR-keyed, captcha-gated, no official bulk API; scraping is common but legally grey). NJDG aggregates pendency and disposal statistics. IBBI quarterly newsletters give realization and haircut data per resolved CIRP (about 1,000+ resolution plans, about 2,500+ liquidations). NCLT and DRT cause lists and orders cover about 3.5M Section 138 cheque-bounce cases and the DRT recovery suits. Labels: recovery percentage, time to recovery, and the outcomes of SARFAESI enforcement actions.
r2.current_users: Litigation-as-credit-signal is crowded: Perfios Litigation BI, Probe42, Legitquest Litigation Check, InstaFinancials DirectorLegal, AuthBridge and CrimeCheck all sell court-record checks to lenders (verified by search). ARCs (ARCIL, Edelweiss ARC, NARCL) do pricing in-house; ARCs are hiring AI/analytics roles (search result). I found no ML-native buyer of NPA pools.
r2.ml_unlock: Predict the recovery curve (amount and timing) of a stressed loan from the borrower's and guarantors' full litigation graph, the speed of the specific bench (DRT/NCLT benches differ hugely), and the history of collateral enforcement. Use it to bid on bank NPA auctions and ARC security-receipt tranches, or to run outcome-priced collections for NBFCs.
r2.path_to_1B: Indian banks sell tens of thousands of crore of NPAs to ARCs each year, and the cumulative gross stressed book runs to lakhs of crore (memory). An ML-priced ARC/AIF that buys retail and MSME NPA pools, where diligence per loan is the bottleneck, could reach $1B+ AUM and valuation. Data-only SaaS to lenders is commoditized (Perfios et al.) and would not reach $1B. Risks: the RBI ARC licence needs ₹300cr net owned funds, eCourts scraping legality, and slow courts that keep IRRs low.
r2.why_now: eCourts Phase III (₹7,210cr, 2023-27) is digitizing records and moving to e-filing. IBC has about 8 years of resolved outcome labels. RBI's 2024-25 push to allow retail NPA sales and securitization of stressed assets opens new buyer roles.
r2.verified: Verified: the Perfios, Probe42, Legitquest and InstaFinancials litigation products for lenders, and that ARCs are building AI teams. From memory: case counts, IBBI disclosure specifics, eCourts Phase III budget, and RBI rule changes.

r2.name: Outcome prediction and litigation finance on French open-data judgments (Judilibre)
r2.jurisdiction: France
r2.legal_basis: Loi pour une République numérique 2016 (Arts. 20-21) and Loi 2019-222, Art. 33, with the 2020 décret setting a phased schedule. The Cour de cassation publishes all judicial decisions via Judilibre/PISTE; the Conseil d'État does the same for administrative ones. Art. 33 also criminalizes (up to 5 years in prison) using judges' identities to evaluate or predict their individual practices.
r2.dataset: Judilibre API (PISTE) with Cour de cassation, cours d'appel and, under the phased rollout, tribunaux judiciaires decisions, pseudonymized, millions of documents. Administrative-court decisions are on opendata.justice-administrative.fr. Outcomes are in the text, but amounts, parties and judges are partly redacted.
r2.current_users: Very crowded: Doctrine (raised heavily; convicted of illicit pre-open-data scraping, per next.ink), Predictice, Lexbase, Dalloz/Lefebvre, LexisNexis. Case Law Analytics shut down (memory). Litigation funders active in France include Deminor, Omni Bridgeway and Alto. Bans on judge analytics and redaction remove the most valuable features.
r2.ml_unlock: Claim-level win and amount prediction to underwrite contingency funding of mass consumer/employment claims (prud'hommes scales) and newly allowed class actions under the 2025 EU Representative Actions transposition. Incremental, not revolutionary.
r2.path_to_1B: Weak. The French legal-tech market and litigation-funding volumes are small, about €100-200M (memory). Incumbents already own the data products. The legal prohibition on judge-level modelling caps the edge. Unlikely to reach $1B.
r2.why_now: Rollout of first-instance decisions continues to 2025-2027, and LLMs make the pseudonymized text usable. But the incumbents get the same data the same day.
r2.verified: Verified: the Doctrine conviction (next.ink) and Judilibre's existence. From memory: the Art. 33 judge-analytics ban, the rollout schedule, the Case Law Analytics closure, and market size.

r2.name: Chinese court judgments (China Judgments Online) as a credit and enforcement-risk signal
r2.jurisdiction: China
r2.legal_basis: SPC Provisions on the Publication of Judgments Online (2013, revised 2016) required publication of most judgments. Since January 2024 the SPC has moved to an internal-only National Court Judgments Database for court staff, and public CJO uploads have sharply declined.
r2.dataset: CJO peaked at 140M+ documents. Public access is now shrinking and rate-limited, and bulk scraping is illegal under the Data Security Law and anti-crawling enforcement. Historical dumps circulate (e.g. the Wikimedia preservation effort) but are legally toxic for a company.
r2.current_users: Domestic incumbents have built litigation-risk credit signals on it for years: Tianyancha, Qichacha, Qixinbao, Wolters Kluwer China, PKULaw, Alibaba/Ant risk control, and courts' own Smart Court AI. The dishonest-judgment-debtor (失信被执行人) list is already standard in credit scoring.
r2.ml_unlock: Litigation-graph credit underwriting for SMEs. It already exists domestically, and a foreign founder cannot get the data.
r2.path_to_1B: Not viable for a YC company: data access is closing, legal risk is high, and incumbents are entrenched.
r2.why_now: The opposite: the window is closing (2023-24 restrictions).
r2.verified: Verified by search: the December 2023 to 2024 restriction to an internal database (RFA, SCMP, China Justice Observer, Donald Clarke). From memory: the incumbent list and document counts.

r2.name: Commercial-court insolvency outcomes from Indonesia's Direktori Putusan (with notes on Germany and Mexico)
r2.jurisdiction: Indonesia (Germany and Mexico noted)
r2.legal_basis: Indonesia: Supreme Court Chief Justice Decree 1-144/KMA/SK/I/2011 on information disclosure and Law 14/2008 on Public Information require online publication of decisions; the Direktori Putusan Mahkamah Agung (putusan3.mahkamahagung.go.id) holds about 10M+ decisions (memory). Germany: a constitutional duty to publish decisions exists (BVerwG 1997), but under 1% of decisions are published, there is no bulk regime, and the 2024-25 Justice Ministry data-access initiative is not in force. Mexico: Ley General de Transparencia Art. 73 requires public versions of judgments, but bulk access is scattered across 32 state judiciaries.
r2.dataset: Indonesia: HTML/PDF decisions including Commercial Court (Pengadilan Niaga) PKPU debt-suspension and bankruptcy cases, scrapeable, with labels (homologation/composition approved vs. bankruptcy). Germany and Mexico: thin, non-bulk.
r2.current_users: Indonesia: Hukumonline (Pro/Analytics) and a few legal-search tools. I know of no ML underwriter using PKPU outcomes. Germany: Juris, Beck, Wolters Kluwer, and OpenJur/OpenLegalData (non-profit).
r2.ml_unlock: Predict PKPU outcomes and creditor recovery for Indonesian private-credit and fintech-lending exposures, and price distressed claims. Germany and Mexico lack the volume of labeled data.
r2.path_to_1B: Weak. Indonesian distressed-debt trading is shallow and the data is noisy. At most a niche tool inside a private-credit fund, and no visible path to $1B. Germany and Mexico: no bulk data, no edge.
r2.why_now: Indonesia's P2P lending defaults and the 2023-25 PKPU surge create demand, but the market is still small.
r2.verified: All from memory; no searches spent on this lane.

r2.name: Component-failure hazard engine for vehicle service contracts (VSC) and warranty underwriting, trained on UK MOT + Dutch APK defect histories
r2.jurisdiction: UK (DVSA MOT), Netherlands (RDW APK). The product is sold into the US/UK warranty and VSC market.
r2.legal_basis: UK Road Traffic Act 1988 s.45-47 requires an annual MOT for cars over 3 years old, and DVSA publishes every test result (pass/fail, odometer, itemised advisories and defects) as anonymised bulk open data and through the MOT History API (keyed by registration). Dutch Wegenverkeerswet: periodic APK, and RDW publishes per-plate 'Geconstateerde Gebreken' (defects found) as open data under CC0.
r2.dataset: MOT: about 40M tests a year since 2005, so 500M+ records. Each has vehicle make/model/engine/fuel, first-use date, odometer reading, test result and free-text plus coded defect and advisory items (brakes, suspension, corrosion, emissions, etc.). Bulk annual CSVs come from data.gov.uk/DVSA, and per-VRM lookups need API registration. RDW: about 10M vehicles, with per-plate APK date, defect codes and odometer judgement, on opendata.rdw.nl through the Socrata API. Together these give a longitudinal panel of component degradation for each vehicle, sorted by model, engine, age and mileage. That is a survival dataset no OEM or warranty company has outside its own book.
r2.current_users: Consumer lookup and 'AI risk' tools are crowded and low-value: CarIntellect, Carhunch, Car Guide (just-auto interview on AI predicting parts failures), PlateInsight, HPI/Cap HPI, Experian and Autotrader UK show MOT history. UK insurers use MOT mileage through LexisNexis/Experian enrichment. I found no evidence that anyone uses MOT/APK defect survival curves to price VSC or warranty risk at the component level. That is unverified, because incumbents such as Assurant, APCO and Fortegra keep their actuarial inputs private.
r2.ml_unlock: Survival or hazard models giving P(component X fails before mileage or age Y) for each make/model/engine/trim, conditioned on that vehicle's own defect trajectory (for example a corrosion advisory at year 6 predicts a suspension failure at year 8). Outputs are a per-VIN expected repair cost and a fair warranty premium. Some of it transfers to the US for the same platforms (Ford, Toyota, VW, BMW, Tesla), and it can be calibrated against NHTSA complaints. It can also act as a 'condition oracle' that adjusts residual value for lenders and auction houses.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers: VSC administrators and insurers, dealers' F&I, auto lenders, and fintech warranty sellers (CarShield, Endurance, Olive). The US VSC market is roughly $40-50B in annual retail sales (industry estimates from market-research reports, not verified precisely), and the UK used-car warranty market is about £1-2B. Path to $1B: become an MGA or program carrier that writes your own VSC, with risk ceded to reinsurers, priced by the model, and capture the 20-40% margins that VSC carries. A data-moat underwriter like this resembles a 'Lemonade/Root for car warranties'. Weaknesses: the data is UK/NL-specific, US vehicle mixes differ, and the MOT records failures found at inspection, not repair cost.
r2.why_now: The DVSA moved to a new MOT History API in 2024-25 with registration. RDW open data is mature (Socrata). Used-car ages are at record highs (US average 12.6 yrs), so VSC attach rates are rising. EV and hybrid failure modes (brakes, tyres and suspension wear differently because of weight) are now showing up in MOT data, and incumbent actuarial tables lack them. LLMs can normalise the free-text defect descriptions.
r2.verified: Search verified that consumer MOT-AI tools exist (CarIntellect, Carhunch, Car Guide) and that RDW publishes per-plate defects ('Open Data RDW: Geconstateerde Gebreken' on data.overheid.nl). From memory: the MOT bulk data and its fields, the legal sections, and the VSC market size (search returned only market-research pages, so treat $40-50B as approximate).

r2.name: Japan bridge/tunnel deterioration model to bid on or underwrite performance-based maintenance contracts
r2.jurisdiction: Japan (MLIT). The model could later be extended to the US NBI.
r2.legal_basis: The 2014 amendment to the Road Act ordinance (道路法施行規則) and MLIT notice require a close visual inspection every 5 years of all road bridges at least 2m long (about 730k) and all tunnels (about 11k), rated in soundness classes I-IV. Results are compiled nationally in the 全国道路施設点検データベース (xROAD), and the JBEC road-bridge DB exposes a public API for periodic inspection data. US: 23 CFR 650 Subpart C (NBIS) requires biennial inspections, published as the National Bridge Inventory (about 620k bridges, with component condition ratings since 1992).
r2.dataset: Japan: per-bridge records (structure type, age, location, traffic, coastal/salt exposure), soundness grade, member-level damage, and photos in inspection reports. Cycle 2 (2019-23) is complete and cycle 3 is under way, so there are two or three labelled observations per asset. US NBI: 30+ years of annual condition ratings, a long panel.
r2.current_users: Heavily studied in academia (NBI deterioration Markov models are decades old). Commercial: Bentley/AASHTOWare BrM, Deighton, and Japanese firms (NEC, Fujitsu, Pasco, Kozo Keikaku) run inspection-AI and drone-imagery projects. MLIT's own NILIM builds deterioration models. The space is crowded on the software side.
r2.ml_unlock: Forecasting deterioration per bridge and per member across Japan's dense, labelled national panel. The delinquency, guaranty-purchase and liquidation statuses are new in 2026 and will build a monthly panel if they keep being refreshed. You can join it to PPP (11M+ loans with forgiveness and fraud flags), state business registries, UCC filings, Google/Yelp reviews, foot traffic and permits, because the borrower's name and address are public. r2.ml_unlock: A default and loss-given-default model for small businesses, trained on about 30 years of SBA outcomes across every lender, industry, franchise brand and ZIP. It would also learn from location features (competitor density, foot traffic, lease, review trajectory) linked through the public borrower address. No single lender sees more than its own book. The new monthly delinquency statuses add early-warning labels (who goes DELINQ to PURCH), not just final outcomes. Products: (1) a site- and brand-level 'will this franchise location survive' score; (2) pricing for the unguaranteed 25-50% portion and for non-SBA SMB loans; (3) servicing triage for existing SBA lenders.

Unguaranteed portions are $8-12B/yr of risk that lenders hold, and the US SMB lending market is about $1.4T outstanding. Routes to $1B+: (a) acquire or partner with an SBLC, or buy a small bank as Live Oak's playbook did, and originate with a better loss model; SBA lenders earn about 8-10% premiums selling guaranteed strips plus servicing spread. (b) A fund that buys unguaranteed portions and SMB loan pools, priced with the model. (c) Data and risk-score SaaS sold to about 1,500 SBA lenders as the wedge. Live Oak and Newtek show that SBA-centric lenders reach $1-3B market caps.
r2.why_now: SBA started publishing loan-level delinquency, purchase and liquidation statuses in 2026, the first time live outcome labels have been public. SBA policy is in flux (SOP 50 10 8 tightened underwriting in 2025, fee changes, and the SBLC licensing reopening and then retrenchment), and 7(a) defaults are rising after the 2021-23 vintages. LLMs can now cheaply resolve borrower names and addresses to web and alternative data.

r2.name: NEM competitor-strategy twin: inverse-RL on every unit's published bids to run autonomous battery bidding / a prop trading desk
r2.jurisdiction: Australia (NEM: QLD, NSW, VIC, SA, TAS)
r2.legal_basis: National Electricity Rules / AEMO market transparency: every scheduled unit's 10 price bands, band volumes and every rebid (with a mandatory rebid reason) are published next day (MMS Data Model, BIDPEROFFER/BIDDAYOFFER tables) at 5-minute dispatch resolution, tied to the participant's identity. AER Rebidding and Technical Parameters Guideline governs the rebid reasons and is under review in 2026.
r2.dataset: NEMWeb / MMS Data Model archive: unit-level bids and rebids with participant names, dispatch targets, FCAS (8 markets) enablement, 5-minute prices, constraints and interconnector flows, going back to about 2009. Free CSV/zip; tens of TB uncompressed. Outcome labels are included: price, dispatch and revenue for each unit.
r2.current_users: Very crowded. Battery optimisers/autobidders such as Tesla Autobidder, Fluence Mosaic, Habitat Energy, Edify, Gridcog, Akaysha, Iberdrola, Shell Energy, Enel X and in-house desks at AGL/Origin/EnergyAustralia (Modo keeps a directory of about 20 NEM optimisers). ez2view/NEMreview (Global-Roam/WattClarity) shows the bid data. Modo publishes autobidder league tables. Academics already model competitor bids (arXiv 2607.13002, 'Shared Bidding Algorithms and Competition', July 2026, uses NEM data on shared autobidders).
r2.ml_unlock: A behavioural model of each rival, learned with inverse-RL from about 15 years of identified bids and rebids, predicts how every portfolio will rebid given the state of the system. That gives you a game-theoretic look-ahead (a price-maker policy) instead of a price forecast. The real edge is anticipating late rebids and strategic withholding during price spikes, which sets most NEM battery revenue.
r2.path_to_1B: Optimisation SaaS in the NEM is a fee of about 5-10% of battery revenue. NEM BESS revenue is a few $B AUD a year by about 2030 and shared among 20+ optimisers, so as SaaS it is a niche of roughly $100-300M. The $1B route is to take risk: run a merchant trading house or tolling desk that offers fixed tolls to battery owners and keeps the upside. That needs a balance sheet and an AFSL/NEM registration, and you would compete with Tesla, Fluence and the gentailers.
r2.why_now: NEM batteries went from about 1 GW to more than 10 GW of committed capacity in 2024-26. Algorithmic bidders now set the price in many intervals, so a model of the other algorithms is worth more than a weather or price model. The AER is reviewing rebidding rules over AI and collusion concerns.
r2.verified: Searched and found: Modo directory of NEM optimisers/autobidders, the arXiv 2607.13002 paper on shared bidding algorithms in electricity markets, and the AER 2026 Rebidding Guideline review (Origin submission dated March 2026). r2.name: Bid-level structural simulator to underwrite merchant storage and renewables (revenue floors, tolls, revenue puts)
r2.jurisdiction: Multi-market: NEM (identified bids next day), ERCOT (60-day SCED/DAM offer curves by resource), PJM/MISO/CAISO/SPP/NYISO/ISO-NE (masked offers with a lag of about 3-4 months), GB BM (BOAs and bid/offer prices published by BMU via Elexon)

FERC-approved ISO tariff provisions for publishing masked offer data. NER (Australia). The BSC (Balancing and Settlement Code) in GB publishes Balancing Mechanism bids and offers by unit.

r2.current_users: Crowded on the analytics side: Aurora, Ascend Analytics (incl. the 'Ensurance' revenue-insurance product), Energy Exemplar PLEXOS, Modo indices, Tyba, Enspired, GridBeyond, Yes Energy. On the risk side: Nephila/Ascend-style revenue puts, Statkraft, Octopus, Engie and Gresham House as counterparties for floors and tolls (e.g. Gresham House floor deals on 789 MW in GB, 2025). Most models are fundamental or statistical price simulators; agent-based models of how individual bidders behave as the fleet changes are mostly academic.
r2.ml_unlock: An agent-based market twin. Each existing and future participant is a learned bidding policy (inverse-RL on disclosed offers). You then simulate the price distribution as 20-50 GW of new batteries arrive, which is exactly the cannibalisation risk lenders cannot price today. Historical forecasts can be backtested against realised spreads, giving a calibrated tail. That lets you write 10-year floors cheaper or more safely than incumbents.
r2.path_to_1B: The buyers are merchant BESS developers, project lenders, tax-equity investors and insurers. Global BESS additions are roughly $50-100B of capex a year by the late 2020s (BNEF-style estimates, from memory), and most projects need a floor or toll to raise debt. Earning a 2-5% premium on contracted revenue, or the spread on tolls held in your own book, is a market in the billions. A risk-taking company of the Ascend Ensurance or Nephila type could reach $1B+ only by putting its own balance sheet behind it (or reinsurance capacity) and winning the model-accuracy war.
r2.why_now: Merchant battery buildout in ERCOT, NEM and GB outpaces the supply of tolls. Lenders worry about revenue cannibalisation, floors are becoming standard (2024-26), and a model of how the fleet behaves is the missing piece.
r2.verified: Searched and found: Ascend Analytics Ensurance (revenue insurance), Gresham House/Statkraft 789 MW floor agreements, Enspired BESS financing, and GridStatus/Yes Energy/Modo offering ERCOT 60-day data. From memory: the BESS capex size, the masking lag, and ERCOT protocol section numbers.
