r2.name: Cross-market unit-failure model from mandatory outage disclosures (REMIT UMMs + NEM/ERCOT outages) for outage-risk trading and insurance
r2.jurisdiction: EU/UK (REMIT Art. 4 inside-information disclosure, ENTSO-E Transparency Reg. 543/2013), plus NEM MT PASA unit availability and ERCOT outage reports
r2.legal_basis: EU REMIT obliges participants to publish every planned or unplanned unavailability of 100 MW or more within an hour (UMMs). Regulation 543/2013 requires per-unit generation and outage data on the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform. Note: EU order books (EPEX/Nord Pool) and REMIT transaction data are NOT public; only aggregated curves are, so bid-level inverse-RL is impossible in Europe.
r2.dataset: About 10 years of per-unit forced and planned outages, with start/end times, MW and cause text, for about 3,000 large EU units. NEM/ERCOT have equivalent availability data. Labels are failure events and their duration.
r2.current_users: Trading data vendors already ingest UMMs in real time (Montel, Volue Insight, Kpler/LSEG, Bloomberg, Energy Quantified), and commodity desks model outage duration. Plant insurers (HSB/Munich Re, FM Global) use their own loss data instead.
r2.ml_unlock: A hazard model that forecasts forced outages and how long they will last, for every disclosed unit of every rival, trained across the fleet. Trading the expected outage before it is announced, or pricing outage-duration risk, is something no single owner can do because each sees only its own units.
r2.path_to_1B: As a feature for trading desks it is a commodity data niche. As machinery-breakdown underwriting for gas, nuclear, coal and wind fleets (a market of several $B in global power-plant insurance premiums, from memory), it has a credible but slow path through an MGA. Overlaps with what was rejected before (predictive maintenance / nuclear engineering), so it is borderline.
r2.why_now: Ageing thermal fleets, the French nuclear outage shock of 2022, and record outage-driven price spikes make outage risk the main driver of price tails in the EU.
r2.verified: From memory only (REMIT Art. 4, Reg 543/2013, and the fact that EPEX/Nord Pool publish only aggregate curves while JEPX and India IEX publish only aggregate bid stacks, not unit bids). Not verified by search because of the budget.

r2.name: Patent-example formulation foundation model (battery electrolytes, cathodes, alloys, polymers, catalysts): predict properties of unseen formulations and suggest designs around claims
r2.jurisdiction: Global (USPTO, EPO, CNIPA, JPO, KIPO); CNIPA now the largest source of battery examples
r2.legal_basis: 35 USC 112(a) enablement and written description; EPC Art. 83; CN Patent Law Art. 26. Applicants must publish working examples to get a monopoly. Applications publish after 18 months (35 USC 122(b)).
r2.dataset: Tens of millions of full-text patents. Worked examples and tables give compositions, process conditions and measured properties (capacity retention after N cycles, conductivity, yield strength, turnover frequency). Free bulk XML from USPTO ODP and EPO DocDB/full text. CNIPA full text is available through vendors.
r2.current_users: Heavily mined already. NextMove Pistachio (reactions from patents), CAS/SciFinder, Elsevier Reaxys (includes patent examples), and PatSnap Eureka, which markets AI electrolyte formulation built on patent data. Citrine Informatics, Aionics, Chemix, SES AI 'Molecular Universe' and ByteDance Research (arXiv 2504.18728, electrolyte models) do ML on similar data. Materials-LLM startups (Periodic Labs, Lila, CuspAI, Orbital Materials) are also nearby.
r2.ml_unlock: A model trained on patent examples that predicts the measured property of a new recipe and maps claim scope, so R&D teams can find white space and design-arounds. Weakness: patent examples are selectively reported, mostly successes, and are often written to be hard to reproduce, so the labels are biased and noisy. The disclosure has no failure labels.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers are cell makers, chemical and materials majors and agrochemical companies. Materials-informatics software is roughly a $100-300M/yr market per various analyst reports (memory, unverified), which is the niche size already rejected. A $1B outcome would need the company to become a materials developer that licenses IP, which is a long, capital-heavy path. CAS and Elsevier own distribution.
r2.why_now: LLM extraction from tables and figures makes structured parsing of examples cheap. Chinese battery patent volume is very large. But incumbents saw the same thing at the same time.
r2.verified: Search confirmed PatSnap's AI electrolyte-formulation marketing and the ByteDance electrolyte paper. Pistachio, Reaxys, CAS, Citrine and Aionics are from memory. The market size is from memory and unverified.

r2.name: Patent validity underwriter: price the chance a patent survives challenge, then take the risk (patent litigation insurance, litigation finance or patent acquisition)
r2.jurisdiction: US (PTAB, district courts, ITC); later EPO oppositions and the UPC
r2.legal_basis: 35 USC 122 makes file wrappers public once an application publishes, including every office action, examiner-cited prior art, amendment and interview summary. AIA 2012 created IPR/PGR, and every petition, institution decision and final written decision is public. Court dockets are public through PACER. Rejections must be stated on the record under 35 USC 132.
r2.dataset: Many millions of office actions with structured 102/103/112 rejections and cited art. The USPTO Office Action Research Dataset covers 2008-2017, and an Office Action Rejection API now runs on ODP. About 1,200-1,500 IPR petitions a year since 2012, with institution and claim-by-claim outcomes (more than 15,000 labeled cases). District court invalidity rulings and Federal Circuit affirmance rates add more. These are real outcome labels: whether a claim survived an expert challenge, and against what art.
r2.current_users: Analytics: Lex Machina (LexisNexis), Docket Navigator, Juristat and LexisNexis PatentAdvisor (prosecution outcomes), Unified Patents (PTAB data plus a defensive membership model), RPX (defensive aggregator; went private in 2018 for about $555M, from memory). Patlytics and Solve Intelligence (well-funded AI patent tools) work on drafting, infringement and invalidity search, not underwriting. Academic ML exists (Berkeley 2017 'Predicting Bad Patents'; Drexel IPR institution prediction). Burford, Fortress and Parabellum fund patent cases with human diligence. I found no company that uses an ML validity model to write insurance or buy patents at scale, but I verified that only lightly.
r2.ml_unlock: An adversarial validity model. Given a claim set, it finds the strongest prior-art combination (trained on examiner and PTAB citation choices) and outputs a calibrated survival probability by claim, by venue and by panel. Combined with an infringement-exposure estimate, that gives an expected value per patent. No single law firm, funder or insurer sees all the outcomes in a consistent, structured form.
r2.path_to_1B: Take risk rather than sell SaaS. US patent litigation finance is a multi-billion-dollar segment of roughly $15-20B litigation-finance AUM (memory). Patent defense costs run about $2-5M+ per case to trial (AIPLA survey, memory). Products: (a) insurance against invalidation or defense costs, written as an MGA with a capacity partner; (b) funding plaintiff cases or buying portfolios cheaply after scoring them; (c) defensive memberships priced by model. RPX reached about $300M/yr revenue at its peak (memory). Underwriting income at scale, plus balance-sheet returns, gives a credible $1B path. Risks: legal-regime volatility (USPTO discretionary-denial changes in 2025 cut IPR institution sharply) and slow capital cycles.
r2.why_now: USPTO moved bulk data and APIs to the Open Data Portal (2024-25). LLMs can now read full file wrappers and prior-art PDFs. Rules changed in 2025: discretionary denials rose and IPR became harder to get, which repriced patent risk overnight. Litigation funders are under pressure to show quantitative underwriting.
r2.verified: Search confirmed the Office Action Research Dataset and the rejection API, plus the academic PTAB-prediction work. Competitor scope (Patlytics, Unified Patents, RPX), market sizes and the 2025 discretionary-denial shift are from memory.

r2.name: Generic-entry / loss-of-exclusivity forecaster that trades or finances on its own predictions (Orange Book + Paragraph IV + PTAB + ANDA)
r2.jurisdiction: US (FDA, district courts in Delaware and New Jersey, PTAB); the EU SPC registers are an extension
r2.legal_basis: Hatch-Waxman (21 USC 355(b)(1), (j)(2)(A)(vii)(IV)) forces brands to list patents in the Orange Book, and generics must publicly certify against them. FDA publishes the Paragraph IV certification list, including first-filer dates. The 30-month stay and 180-day exclusivity are statutory. BPCIA patent dance for biologics (Purple Book). Settlements must be filed with the FTC under the MMA 2003. FTC publishes only aggregates, but entry dates often appear in disclosures.
r2.dataset: Orange Book (patents, use codes, exclusivities; downloadable). Paragraph IV list. PACER Hatch-Waxman dockets (about 300-500 cases a year). PTAB pharma IPRs. ANDA approval and tentative-approval dates. Patent file wrappers. Outcome labels come from about 20 years of litigated outcomes, settlement entry dates and launch-at-risk events.
r2.current_users: Hedge funds and generics companies do this in-house with lawyers. DrugPatentWatch, Evaluate, Citeline/Cortellis, IQVIA and Clarivate sell databases and expert forecasts. Royalty Pharma and others underwrite royalties partly on LOE timing. No dominant ML-native forecaster is known (memory, unverified).
r2.ml_unlock: A probabilistic LOE date per molecule that combines claim-level validity (trained on Hatch-Waxman and PTAB outcomes), judge and venue effects, settlement-pattern priors (first-filer economics), and FDA approval timing. It forecasts revenue cliffs better than sell-side consensus.
r2.path_to_1B: (a) Data sold to roughly 500 pharma-focused funds and BD teams at $100-500k/yr, which is a modest market. (b) The bigger path is taking positions: royalty and synthetic-royalty financing priced on better LOE curves (the royalty market deploys about $5-10B/yr; Royalty Pharma alone has about $2.5B+ revenue, from memory), or a fund strategy, or funding generic challengers' Paragraph IV litigation for a share of 180-day exclusivity profits. Biosimilars and the 2025-2032 patent cliff (about $200-300B of brand revenue at risk, a common industry estimate) give a large addressable pool.
r2.why_now: The 2025-2032 LOE cliff is the largest ever. IRA price negotiation interacts with LOE timing. LLMs make claim-construction and file-wrapper parsing cheap. The FTC push to delist improper Orange Book patents (2023-24) changes listings.
r2.verified: From memory: Hatch-Waxman legal basis, data sources and competitor landscape. I did not search-verify market numbers.

r2.name: Antibody patent-sequence FTO and design-around engine (WIPO ST.26 sequence listings)
r2.jurisdiction: Global (USPTO, EPO, WIPO PCT, CNIPA)
r2.legal_basis: Sequence-listing rules (37 CFR 1.831+, WIPO ST.26 mandatory since July 2022) force machine-readable disclosure of every claimed antibody, VHH and peptide sequence. Enablement and written description (Amgen v. Sanofi, 2023) push applicants to disclose more species and functional data.
r2.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of patented antibody sequences with target, epitope and sometimes affinity data. PLAbDab holds about 150k+ patent and literature antibodies, plus a nanobody version.
r2.current_users: Oxford OPIG PLAbDab (free, academic). PatSnap Bio, CAS, GenomeQuest/LifeQuest (Clarivate) and STN sequence search. AI antibody companies (Absci, BigHat, Generate, Chai, Nabla, Xaira) already use patent sequences for training and novelty filtering. Crowded.
r2.ml_unlock: Claim-scope-aware generation: design binders that are predicted functional and fall outside every claim's sequence-identity or CDR scope, with FTO risk scores. After Amgen, genus claims are weaker, so design-arounds are easier and more valuable.
r2.path_to_1B: Becomes a feature inside AI biologics platforms and CROs. A standalone FTO software market is small, under $200M. The $1B path is only as a drug-design company, which is a different business and is crowded.
r2.why_now: ST.26 is fully machine-readable as of 2022. Amgen v. Sanofi narrowed functional genus claims.
r2.verified: Search confirmed PLAbDab and PLAbDab-nano. ST.26 date and Amgen v. Sanofi are from memory. The AI-antibody competitor list is from memory.

r2.name: Patent-collateral lending using USPTO assignment, security-interest, maintenance-fee and abandonment records as outcome labels
r2.jurisdiction: US
r2.legal_basis: 35 USC 261 says unrecorded assignments are void against later purchasers, so transfers and security interests are recorded publicly at the USPTO Assignment database. Maintenance fees under 35 USC 41(b) are due at 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years, and payment or expiry status is public. That gives a revealed-preference label: the owner chose whether keeping the patent was worth the fee.
r2.dataset: About 10M+ recorded assignment documents, including security agreements, releases and foreclosure-type transfers; maintenance-fee events (bulk download); PTAB and litigation outcomes; reassignment to NPEs, which signals monetization value.
r2.current_users: Patent valuation and analytics: Ocean Tomo (and the old Ocean Tomo 300 index), PatSnap, IPwe (struggled), GreyB, Aon IP Solutions (IP-backed lending advisory), and Barker (raised $3.5M for warrantied AI valuations for asset-backed lending). Lenders such as Fortress and Atlas use IP collateral with human valuation.
r2.ml_unlock: A model of a patent's recovery value in default, trained on what happened to patents of previously failed borrowers: sold or abandoned, sale prices where recorded, and later assertion. It underwrites venture debt for IP-heavy startups.
r2.path_to_1B: Venture debt is about $30-50B/yr in the US (memory). An IP-collateral lender that prices patents better could write a large loan book, but recovery prices are thinly observed and most sale prices are not public, so the labels are weak. Moderate potential.
r2.why_now: USPTO assignment and maintenance data are now on ODP APIs. Higher rates and the SVB collapse in 2023 pushed founders toward alternative collateral.
r2.verified: Search found Barker's funding and an AI patent-valuation landscape. Legal provisions and data volumes are from memory.

r2.name: FOAK Tech-Risk Underwriter: ML on forced final reports from public R&D (OSTI, ARPA-E, CORDIS, UK GtR, SBIR) used to price technology performance insurance and FOAK project debt
r2.jurisdiction: US (DOE/OSTI, ARPA-E, NSF, SBIR), EU (Horizon/CORDIS), UK (UKRI Gateway to Research)
r2.legal_basis: US: DOE awards must deliver final and interim technical reports to OSTI as a condition of the grant (2 CFR 910 / DOE O 241.1, DOE AL/FAL terms; announced via OSTI E-Link), and these are made public unless protected-data periods apply (often up to 5 yrs SBIR data rights, then released). EU: Horizon 2020/Europe Grant Agreement Art. 17/29 requires public deliverables and periodic reports, published on CORDIS. UK: UKRI requires outcomes reporting (Researchfish), published on GtR. Private companies that take public money are forced to disclose milestones, performance figures and failures they would never publish.
r2.dataset: OSTI.gov: ~3M+ records, including tens of thousands of final technical reports from industry awardees (PDF, API). ARPA-E project pages plus 'Impact' tracking with follow-on funding labels. CORDIS: ~35k+ H2020/HE projects with deliverables (PDF), results packs and open data dumps (CSV/JSON). GtR: ~100k+ projects with outcomes (API). SBIR.gov: ~200k awards with Phase I to II to III transitions. The labels come from joining: stated targets vs achieved performance (efficiency, yield, cost per unit, TRL), whether the next phase or follow-on money arrived, and later commercial outcome (plants built, bankruptcies, LPO loans, SEC filings).
r2.current_users: Text analytics on OSTI/CORDIS exists only for research-intelligence uses (Dimensions, Elsevier SciVal, Clarivate, CORDIS's own tools). Technology performance insurance for FOAK climate projects is a real but thin market led by New Energy Risk (an MGA backed by large reinsurers; Biofuels Digest ran a 2026 'Guide to Technology Performance Insurance'), plus Munich Re's performance guarantees. Neither is known to systematically mine the public-R&D report corpus as an actuarial base. No one is known to treat it as a loss-history dataset.
r2.ml_unlock: The first actuarial base rate for 'does novel technology X hit nameplate at scale.' An LLM extraction pipeline turns about 30 years of forced final reports into structured (technology class, scale step, target metric, achieved metric, time slip, cost overrun) tuples. A model then predicts the probability a given FOAK plant (electrolyzer, SAF, DAC, long-duration storage, advanced geothermal, green steel) reaches X% of nameplate within Y months, given its lineage of public-funded predecessors. That is the missing piece of FOAK finance: lenders (DOE LPO, infra funds, banks) won't lend because tech risk can't be priced, and insurers price it by hand, one deal at a time.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers and positions: (1) be the MGA/carrier writing technology performance insurance and earn premium plus float. Each FOAK project is $100M-$2B of capex, and a performance wrap is typically ~1-5% of covered value. (2) Sell tech-risk ratings to project lenders, LPO and climate infra funds, like a Moody's for FOAK. Market: IEA/BNEF estimate demonstration and FOAK climate capex needs of hundreds of billions over the decade. US IRA/LPO alone had >$100B of loan authority (some since rescinded or politically at risk). Even 2% premium on $20B/yr of wrapped capex is $400M/yr GWP, which is a credible $1B+ MGA/insurer valuation. Also extends to defense and space hardware scale-up.
r2.why_now: LLMs can finally read hundreds of thousands of messy PDF final reports and extract quantitative target/achieved pairs. A wave of FOAK climate plants from 2022-2026 is reaching COD, many underperforming, which creates fresh outcome labels. IRA-era project finance needs tech-risk mitigation, and the MGA model lets a startup take risk with reinsurer capacity.
r2.verified: Searched: existence of New Energy Risk and technology performance insurance as an active category (confirmed). From memory (not re-verified this round): OSTI final-report requirement under 2 CFR 910 / DOE O 241.1, CORDIS deliverable publication under Horizon grant agreements, GtR/Researchfish, dataset sizes (approximate), premium rates (approximate).

r2.name: Virtual Certification and Efficiency-Claim Risk: ML on DOE CCMS + DOE enforcement tests + ENERGY STAR verification + EU EPREL + CEC MAEDbS
r2.jurisdiction: US federal (DOE EPCA), California (Title 20), EU (Energy Labelling Reg. 2017/1369, Ecodesign/ESPR 2024/1781)
r2.legal_basis: EPCA (42 USC 6291 et seq.) and 10 CFR 429 require manufacturers to certify every basic model's tested efficiency to DOE (CCMS, public). DOE assessment and enforcement testing results and noncompliance determinations are public. 10 CFR 429.70 allows Alternative Efficiency Determination Methods (AEDMs: simulation instead of physical testing) for many commercial products, validated against test data. ENERGY STAR third-party certification and off-the-shelf verification testing (failures published). California Title 20 requires a MAEDbS listing to sell in CA. EU EPREL holds every energy-labelled product, including a technical-documentation compliance section visible to market surveillance authorities.
r2.dataset: CCMS: about 1M+ certified basic models across ~60 product types (tested efficiency, capacity, ratings; CSV/API). DOE enforcement: hundreds of test reports and penalty notices. ENERGY STAR: ~100k certified products with verification failures. CEC MAEDbS: ~2M+ model listings. EPREL: ~1M+ product models (public part via API). Labels: rated vs verified efficiency, failures, delistings.
r2.current_users: Data aggregators and rebate processors use these lists (AHRI directory, CLEAResult, Franklin Energy, Energy Solutions, product-data firms like ENERGY STAR partners). Test labs (Intertek, UL, CSA, TÜV) do physical testing. HVAC OEMs build their own in-house AEDMs. No known startup sells cross-OEM ML-based AEDM or predicts which listed models will fail verification.
r2.ml_unlock: (a) A cross-manufacturer surrogate model that predicts certified efficiency from a bill of materials/design. Offered as a DOE-validated AEDM service it replaces months of lab testing per model variant, and could become 'certification-as-a-service' for HVAC, heat pumps, motors, transformers and commercial refrigeration. (b) Anomaly detection that flags models whose claimed ratings are physically implausible relative to peers. That serves DOE/EU market surveillance, competitors (Lanham Act challenges) and utilities paying rebates on overstated claims.
r2.path_to_1B: Honest ceiling: weak. Efficiency testing and certification spend for appliances/HVAC is probably low-single-digit $B globally, inside the TIC market (~$250B overall, mostly unrelated). Rebate-fraud detection for utilities is a $10M-100M niche. A $1B path would require expanding into the generative design tool for regulated equipment (an 'Ansys for compliance'), which competes with Ansys/Siemens and OEM in-house teams. Likely another $100-300M niche: fails the market filter unless paired with EU ESPR digital product passports.
r2.why_now: DOE's 2023-2025 test-procedure changes (e.g., heat pump M1 / HSPF2 / SEER2) forced mass re-certification. EU ESPR (2024) and Digital Product Passport rollout from 2027 expand mandated product data. LLMs and surrogate models make cross-category physics-informed prediction feasible.
r2.verified: Not searched this round (budget). From memory: CCMS public database, 10 CFR 429.70 AEDM provisions, ENERGY STAR verification testing, EPREL, MAEDbS, ESPR. Competitor absence not verified.

r2.name: Aircraft Component Reliability Oracle: FAA Service Difficulty Reports + ADs + NTSB + EASA mandatory occurrence reports, used to trade used serviceable material (USM) and underwrite maintenance reserves
r2.jurisdiction: US (FAA), EU (EASA)
r2.legal_basis: 14 CFR 121.703 / 135.415 / 145.221 force air carriers and repair stations to report failures, malfunctions and defects to the FAA. These are published in the Service Difficulty Reporting System (SDRS), and the 2000 SDR rule expanded it. Airworthiness Directives (14 CFR Part 39) are public. EU Reg. 376/2014 mandates occurrence reporting (ECCAIRS, partially public). It is a forced disclosure of private fleet failure data that each operator, lessor and MRO sees only for its own fleet.
r2.dataset: SDRS: about 1.5M+ reports since the 1970s, with free text plus part number, ATA chapter, aircraft make/model/serial, and time since overhaul in some records (downloadable). ADs: about 40k+. Join with registry (N-number), fleet databases and part-number/OEM data to get failure-time labels per part number and operator.
r2.current_users: Academic/NLR/MITRE ML work on SDR classification (e.g., depressurization classifiers on SKYbrary). Airline predictive maintenance runs on private data: Airbus Skywise, Boeing AnalytX, GE/Rolls-Royce engine health. Valuation and appraisal firms (Cirium, IBA, Aviation Week Fleet Discovery) and part marketplaces (ILS, PartsBase, ePlane AI, which raised VC) do pricing, not reliability-driven trading. AerCap, AAR, AJ Walter and VSE trade USM by expertise.
r2.ml_unlock: A cross-fleet hazard model per part number and serial lineage: expected removals, the likelihood of an incoming AD, and remaining-life value. You use it to buy teardown aircraft and USM parts below fair value, price 'power-by-the-hour' component programs, and set lessor maintenance reserves. Treat SDR text as a leading indicator of ADs and OEM service bulletins that will force part demand spikes, then position inventory ahead of time.
r2.path_to_1B: Positions: USM trading (the global USM market is roughly $7-9B/yr, with industry estimates rising toward about $10B by 2030), component PBH/MRO contracts (component MRO is roughly $20B+), and maintenance-reserve underwriting for lessors. A data-advantaged parts trader with $1B+ of revenue at 15-25% gross margin is plausible (AAR, VSE and HEICO aftermarket are multi-$B businesses). However, this is NHTSA-recall-adjacent (rejected in round 1). Data quality is poor (sparse hours/cycles, underreporting), and incumbents hold proprietary teardown data. Capital-intensive.
r2.why_now: The MRO/USM shortage from 2023-2026 (GTF/LEAP durability issues, engine teardowns, record USM prices) means pricing reliability is worth more than ever. LLMs can parse 1.5M free-text SDRs. Engine powder-metal AD campaigns show AD-driven demand shocks.
r2.verified: Searched: SDR rule (Federal Register 2000) and the existence of academic ML on SDRs (confirmed; no startup found trading on it). From memory: CFR section numbers, SDRS size, USM market size (approximate, not verified), competitor list.

r2.name: Defense Transition Predictor: SBIR/STTR + FPDS/OTA awards + DTIC reports, used to lend to or invest in defense-tech startups
r2.jurisdiction: US (DoD, SBA)
r2.legal_basis: The SBIR/STTR statute (15 USC 638) requires public award data (SBIR.gov). FFATA/DATA Act requires public award data (FPDS, USAspending, including Phase III and OTAs, partly). DoD final technical reports go to DTIC (some public after distribution review).
r2.dataset: SBIR.gov: about 200k awards with abstracts. FPDS: every contract action (winner, price, vehicle). USAspending. DTIC public technical reports. Labels: Phase I to II to III transition and program-of-record follow-on dollars.
r2.current_users: Crowded. Govini (DoD analytics, large contracts), GovTribe, GovWin/Deltek, Bloomberg Government, HigherGov, Vannevar Labs. Lending: Leonid Capital Partners already provides data-driven non-dilutive capital to SBIR/defense startups. Endeavour (military BNPL) and Arkenstone Defense ($35M seed, July 2026, defense-tech back office) are adjacent. Defense VCs (Shield, a16z American Dynamism) already screen on this data.
r2.ml_unlock: Predicting which SBIR awardees cross the 'valley of death' into Phase III/program of record, then lending against expected contract flow. The ML is real, but the data is fully public, heavily mined, and the edge is thin.
r2.path_to_1B: Defense-tech VC was about $30-50B/yr in 2025-26 and contract financing is a large adjacent market. But incumbents (Leonid, Govini, defense VCs) already sit on this exact data, so the moat is weak. Not recommended.
r2.why_now: The defense-tech boom (Anduril $61B valuation in May 2026, Hadrian ~ $8B) and DoD acquisition reform favor commercial entrants. Startups face long cash gaps between award and payment.
r2.verified: Searched: existence of competitors (Leonid Capital Partners, Arkenstone Defense seed July 2026, Anduril May 2026 raise confirmed in search results). From memory: statutes, dataset sizes.

r2.name: Vehicle Emissions/Durability Risk: EPA/CARB certification + In-Use Verification Program + Emission Defect Information Reports + EU in-service conformity, used for powertrain warranty/recall risk
r2.jurisdiction: US (EPA, CARB), EU (Reg. 2018/858 type approval, 2017/1151 WLTP / RDE, Euro 7)
r2.legal_basis: Clean Air Act §206/207 and 40 CFR 85.1903 (Emission Defect Information Reports when 25+ vehicles have the same defect). 40 CFR 86.1845 requires manufacturer in-use verification testing (IUVP), and certification test data is published by EPA. CARB Executive Orders and warranty reporting under 13 CCR 2144. EU in-service conformity and market surveillance test results are published, and Euro 7 adds battery durability (SOH) requirements.
r2.dataset: EPA certification test data (about 20+ years, every test group, CSV). IUVP results. EDIRs and voluntary emission recall reports (thousands). CARB EOs. EU type-approval and WLTP values (EEA CO2 monitoring dataset, about 10M+ registrations/yr with per-vehicle data). Euro 7 battery durability data is coming.
r2.current_users: OEM compliance teams, consultancies (ICCT and Emissions Analytics use EU/RDE data for advocacy and indexing), and S&P Mobility/JD Power on reliability. NHTSA-recall analytics (rejected in round 1) is the nearest analog.
r2.ml_unlock: Predict which test groups and powertrains will generate emissions defect reports and recalls, or (Euro 7 / CARB ACC II) battery state-of-health warranty failures. Use that to price extended warranties and EV residual values. The most interesting piece is the mandated EV battery durability disclosure (CARB ACC II requires a battery SOH monitor and 70-75% SOH warranty at 8yr/100k), which creates a labeled battery-degradation dataset to underwrite EV residuals and leases.
r2.path_to_1B: EV residual value and battery warranty risk is a real multi-$B exposure for lessors, captives and warranty providers (the US extended warranty market is roughly $40B+). But battery-health analytics startups (Recurrent, Generational/ACV, Moxion-like) and OEMs already compete, and the regulated disclosure regime is only starting (data mostly arrives in 2027+). Moderate.
r2.why_now: CARB ACC II (MY2026+) and Euro 7 battery durability rules start producing mandated SOH data. Used EV residuals collapsed in 2023-25, so lessors are badly burned.
r2.verified: Not searched (budget). From memory: CFR sections, IUVP, EDIR threshold, ACC II SOH requirements, existence of Recurrent. Exact data availability timelines are unverified.

r2.name: AI surety MGA for public-works contractors, priced on DOT bid tabulations plus bridge and pavement condition panels
r2.jurisdiction: US (all 50 state DOTs; federal-aid highway program; Miller Act and state 'Little Miller Acts')
r2.legal_basis: 23 CFR 635.112-114 requires competitive sealed low-bid letting for federal-aid highway contracts. State procurement law requires every bid opening to be public, so each DOT publishes full bid tabulations: every bidder's unit price on every line item, the winner and the margin. The Miller Act (40 USC 3131) and state Little Miller Acts make performance and payment bonds mandatory on public works, so every contractor who wins needs a surety. NBI (23 CFR 650) and HPMS condition data are public and give a forward view of rehab and replace demand by state and county.
r2.dataset: State DOT bid tabs: roughly $100B+/yr of lettings, typically 10-20+ years of history, about 50 portals plus aggregators (Bid Express/Infotech, Oman). Formats range from PDF and Excel to some APIs. Line-item unit prices for every bidder give labels at the bidder x item x letting level. You can join them to DOT contractor prequalification lists, contractor performance evaluations (public in many states), change orders and final-quantity records (some states), default and termination notices, and mechanic's-lien and payment-bond claim lawsuits (court records). NBI: 620k bridges with annual condition ratings since 1992. HPMS: pavement condition (IRI, cracking).
r2.current_users: Infotech/Bid Express and Oman Systems sell bid-history estimating tools to DOTs and contractors. Dodge/ConstructConnect sell project leads. Surety underwriting is dominated by Travelers, Liberty Mutual, CNA, Zurich and Chubb, which underwrite mainly on CPA-reviewed financials and the agent relationship ('3 Cs'). InRev is a small digital surety MGA ($3.8M raise, Accelerant-backed) that focuses on automating small and commercial bond workflow. I found no evidence it does bid-tab-based risk modeling. Shepherd ($42M, 2026) does construction casualty insurance, not surety. I found no one pricing contract surety from public bid-spread and unit-price behavior.
r2.ml_unlock: Predict contractor default and loss on a specific bonded job. Signals: (a) winner's-curse spread, where a low bid far below the second bid and the engineer's estimate predicts losses; (b) unbalanced-bidding patterns at line-item level; (c) backlog reconstructed from all public wins across states, which is the main driver of surety losses and which no single surety sees fully; (d) the contractor's unit-price drift against market cost indices; (e) the DOT's change-order behavior. Then underwrite small and mid contractors that incumbents reject or price poorly. Second product: a bid-optimization copilot for the same contractors, which feeds proprietary data back in.
r2.path_to_1B: US surety direct written premium is about $8-9B/yr (SFAA; contract surety is about 60-65%, so about $5B; from memory, not verified this session). Loss ratios are historically low (about 15-25%), but losses cluster in default cycles. An MGA writing $500M-1B of premium at 25-30% commission plus profit share is a $1B+ enterprise value. Alternatively, become a carrier, or offer subcontractor default insurance (a $1B+ market, Zurich SDI) and contractor working-capital lending on the same signal. IIJA ($1.2T, of which $550B is new spend through FY2026) plus reauthorization keeps lettings elevated. Bonding capacity is the binding constraint for small DBE contractors, which is a political tailwind.
r2.why_now: IIJA lettings have sharply increased the number of bonded jobs and stretched contractor backlogs, which is the classic setup for a surety default cycle. LLMs make it cheap to parse 50 heterogeneous DOT bid-tab PDFs and contractor evaluations. Fronting carriers and MGA infrastructure (Accelerant, Vesttoo-style capacity) make a new MGA feasible on seed or Series A money.
r2.verified: Verified by search: InRev exists as a surety MGA backed by Accelerant ($3.8M raise), and Shepherd raised $42M for construction insurance AI. From memory: the 23 CFR 635 low-bid requirement, public bid tabs, the Miller Act, the surety premium size, and that no one uses bid-tab spreads for surety pricing. The last point needs founder diligence; ask SFAA and Merchants Bonding.

r2.name: Risk-based bridge inspection interval engine plus an AI-native bridge inspection firm (NBIS 2022 Method 2)
r2.jurisdiction: US (FHWA; about 52 state DOTs, plus local owners of about 50% of bridges)
r2.legal_basis: 23 CFR 650 (NBIS) mandates inspection of every public bridge over 20 ft, normally every 24 months. The 2022 NBIS update (87 FR 27396, May 6 2022) lets owners extend routine intervals to 48 months, and up to 72 months under a 'Method 2' risk assessment panel approved by FHWA, if they justify it with a documented risk analysis. NBI data must be submitted yearly and is published. The new SNBI coding (element-level, roughly 2x the fields) is being phased in, so a fresh, richer label set is arriving.
r2.dataset: NBI: about 620k bridges, annual ASCII/CSV since 1992 (about 30 years x 620k panel), with deck, superstructure, substructure and culvert condition ratings (0-9), posting, scour criticality, ADT, and year built or reconstructed. Element-level data since 2014 for NHS bridges, and SNBI going forward. Joinable public data: NOAA climate and freeze-thaw, deicing-salt exposure proxies, truck-weight (WIM) data, and FEMA flood maps. Failure and closure events are the outcome labels.
r2.current_users: AASHTOWare BrM (deterioration models, Markov-based) and Bentley AssetWise are incumbents. Academic ML on NBI is extensive (Purdue, UMD, Illinois). Drone and AI inspection vendors include Infrastructure Preservation Corp (IPC), Skydio partners, and AssetIntel (SNBI and NBIS software). Big engineering firms (WSP, HNTB, Michael Baker, Stantec) do most consultant inspections. There is no dominant ML-native player that owns Method 2 justifications plus inspection delivery.
r2.ml_unlock: A survival model of component deterioration across 30 years x 620k bridges produces FHWA-acceptable risk scores. These let a DOT legally move low-risk bridges (much of the inventory, especially culverts and young concrete bridges) from 24- to 48- or 72-month cycles, saving tens of millions per state, while concentrating drones, AI defect detection and humans on high-risk structures. Sell it as an outcome-priced service: a share of the inspection-budget savings, or a fixed-price statewide inspection contract that a model-driven firm can win against hourly engineering firms.
r2.path_to_1B: US bridge inspection spend is roughly $1-2B/yr (estimate: about 300k inspections/yr at about $3-6k average, plus far costlier fracture-critical, underwater and NSTM inspections). Bridge rehab and replacement capex is about $15-20B+/yr, with the IIJA Bridge Formula Program at $27.5B. The $1B path is a rolled-up AI-enabled engineering firm (a services-plus-software margin story) expanding into culverts, tunnels, dams, and the international equivalents in Japan and Europe. It is hard: buyers are slow, and inspection must be stamped by a licensed PE and Team Leader.
r2.why_now: The NBIS 2022 rule is the first time US law has rewarded risk models with longer intervals. The SNBI transition forces every state to re-tool its software and data. IIJA money is flowing. Inspector labor is short.
r2.verified: Verified by search: the 2022 NBIS update in the Federal Register (May 6 2022), FHWA interval guidance, and AssetIntel as a SNBI-focused vendor. From memory: the 48/72-month limits, NBI size, and spend estimates. The inspection market size is my estimate, not sourced.

r2.name: Fixed-price lead service line replacement contractor or financier, underwritten by an ML model of the 'unknown' lines
r2.jurisdiction: US (EPA, about 66k community water systems; strongest in IL, MI, NJ, OH, PA, WI and NY)
r2.legal_basis: The EPA Lead and Copper Rule Revisions required every community water system to file a service line inventory by Oct 16 2024. Inventories must be publicly accessible, and systems over 50k must post them online. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (final Oct 2024) require replacing all lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement lines within about 10 years (to about 2037) and periodic inventory updates. Each replacement converts an 'unknown' into a verified material label.
r2.dataset: Public per-address inventories with material (lead, GRR, non-lead or unknown), sometimes with verification method. EPA's 2023 DWINSA estimated about 9.2M lead lines, and early inventories show tens of millions of 'unknown' lines. Joins: parcel year built, tax assessor data, historic plumbing codes, and replacement-program records (outcome labels as excavations happen).
r2.current_users: BlueConduit, the original Flint ML team, is backed by Rockefeller and Google.org. It is used in Detroit (claims about $165M saved) and dozens of utilities, and has a system-level count product. 120Water dominates inventory software (VC-backed). Trinnex (CDM Smith), Jacobs, Black & Veatch and others fold prediction into engineering contracts. So the prediction layer is already taken.
r2.ml_unlock: The only new angle is taking risk: bid fixed-price 'replace every lead line in the city for $X' or 'per-verified-lead-line' contracts, using a better unknown-line model to price, and sequence excavation crews so as few holes as possible are dug at non-lead addresses. Alternatively, finance utilities' replacement programs, since SRF and WIFIA money flows through utilities that need predictable totals.
r2.path_to_1B: Total replacement cost is about $45-90B over the decade (EPA estimated about $20-30B+ for LCRI compliance; real per-line costs run $8-15k). IIJA set aside $15B for LSL replacement through DWSRF. A specialty contractor could reach about $1B in revenue, but as a construction business (low margin, roughly 3-5x EBITDA multiples). Venture-scale is doubtful.
r2.why_now: Inventories went public in Oct 2024. The 10-year LCRI clock started, though compliance dates begin about 2027. Labels accumulate as replacements are done.
r2.verified: Verified by search: BlueConduit's traction (Detroit's estimated $165M savings, Rockefeller and Google.org backing). From memory: the LCRR Oct 2024 deadline, the LCRI 10-year mandate, the 9.2M figure and the $15B IIJA set-aside. Political risk: LCRI litigation or rollback under the current administration is possible; check.

r2.name: Japan mandatory 5-year inspection database as a training corpus for an Asia-wide inspection AI
r2.jurisdiction: Japan (MLIT). Later South Korea (Special Act on Safety Control of Infrastructure) and the EU (Italy after the 2018 Morandi collapse, with ANSFISA guidelines)
r2.legal_basis: After the 2012 Sasago tunnel collapse, MLIT ordinances (2014) require close-up visual inspection of every road bridge over 2 m (about 730k) and every tunnel every 5 years, with a 4-tier soundness judgment (I-IV). Results are aggregated and published in MLIT's national road facility inspection database (opened around 2022, per my memory).
r2.dataset: About 730k bridges plus about 11k tunnels, through 2-plus completed 5-year cycles, with soundness grades. Photo-level records sit with municipalities and are partially accessible. Public access granularity is uncertain.
r2.current_users: Japanese incumbents: NEC, Fujitsu, the Nippon Koei and Pacific Consultants groups, and many municipal drone and AI pilots. Municipal labor shortages are acute (many towns have zero civil engineers), so there is real demand, but procurement is relationship-driven.
r2.ml_unlock: Learn deterioration from 2-3 complete national inspection cycles, then sell 'inspect-by-exception' services to small municipalities that legally must inspect but have no engineers.
r2.path_to_1B: Japan's inspection and maintenance market is a few hundred billion yen per year. A foreign founder's access is weak. Probably a $100-300M outcome unless it becomes a global platform.

r2.name: Other infrastructure-condition datasets in this lane (water main breaks, NID dams, HPMS pavement, FTA NTD transit assets): rejected
r2.jurisdiction: US
r2.legal_basis: NID: the National Dam Safety Program Act (but condition and EAP details are restricted after 9/11). HPMS: 23 CFR 420 and the performance-management rule (23 CFR 490). NTD: 49 USC 5335 plus Transit Asset Management (49 CFR 625). Water main breaks: no federal mandate; only scattered state PUC or open-data portals.

r2.name: Cross-OEM equipment failure underwriter (EU Data Act connected-product data)
r2.jurisdiction: EU/EEA (applies to any product placed on the EU market)
r2.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), applicable since 12 Sept 2025. Arts 3-5: the user of a connected product (machinery, trucks, tractors, construction equipment, compressors, HVAC, medical devices) has a right to the product data and related-service data, and can order the data holder (the OEM) to share it with a third party they choose, on FRAND terms. Gatekeepers under the DMA cannot be recipients. The data-access-by-design duty in Art 3(1) covers products placed on the market from 12 Sept 2026. The receiving third party may not use the data to build a competing product.
r2.dataset: No public dump. The data unlocks per customer: raw sensor streams, fault/DTC codes, operating hours, duty cycles and error logs that OEMs used to keep for their own dealer service networks. A fleet owner (rental company, contractor, farm cooperative, logistics firm) authorizes the startup, which then pulls the data from many OEMs (Caterpillar, Komatsu, Volvo CE, Liebherr, John Deere, CNH, Daimler Truck and others) through each OEM's Data Act portal or API. Proemion and others already sell Data Act portals to OEMs, so access paths are being standardized. The labels are failures, unplanned downtime, and repair events matched to telemetry, gathered across brands: no single OEM can see this, and no single fleet has enough of it.
r2.current_users: Dealer and OEM-captive telematics (CAT VisionLink, Deere Operations Center, Komatsu Komtrax) are single-brand. Mixed-fleet aggregators include Trackunit (Denmark, large), Uptake (US, predictive maintenance, has struggled), Caruso Dataplace and High Mobility (vehicle data marketplaces), and Proemion (OEM-side Data Act compliance). I know of no one using Data Act rights to take risk, i.e. to underwrite fixed-price uptime or maintenance contracts across brands.
r2.ml_unlock: A failure-hazard model trained across brands and fleets that predicts component-level failure probability and remaining useful life for heavy equipment. The company then sells fixed-price, OEM-independent 'uptime guarantees' or extended warranties and breakdown insurance, and prices them better than OEM warranty arms, which only see their own brand. It can also route the predicted repairs to independent service shops, taking share from dealer aftermarket margins, which is exactly the lock-in the Data Act was written to break.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers are equipment rental companies (United Rentals-scale firms; the European rental market is about EUR 30B+ a year), contractors, ag co-ops and truck fleets. Revenue would come from warranty and maintenance-contract premiums plus routing fees on parts and service. Global construction and ag equipment aftermarket service runs in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year (OEMs report roughly 20-30% of revenue from aftermarket; from memory, not checked against a source), and extended warranty on heavy equipment and commercial trucks is a multi-billion-dollar line in the EU alone. A 1-2% share of EU heavy-equipment and truck maintenance contracts underwritten as a program carrier/MGA is enough for a $1B+ valuation. It is an insurtech/MGA model with an exclusive data edge.
r2.why_now: The Data Act became applicable in Sept 2025, and access-by-design for new products started Sept 2026. OEMs are only now standing up the portals, and the case law and FRAND pricing are still unsettled, so a startup that builds the multi-OEM connectors and the claims data first gets a lead that compounds. The risks: OEMs will drag their feet and charge 'reasonable compensation' fees; the trade-secret carve-out (Art 4(6)-(8)) lets them withhold some data; and the Commission's Digital Omnibus may soften parts of the Act.
r2.verified: Searched: the Data Act's Sept 2025 applicability and third-party access, and Proemion offering Data Act portals to OEMs. From memory: the gatekeeper exclusion, the Sept 2026 by-design date, the trade-secret carve-outs, the competitor list, and the market sizes (aftermarket share, rental market size) have not been checked against a source.

r2.name: EV battery residual-value underwriter (EU Battery Regulation BMS access + Battery Passport)
r2.jurisdiction: EU
r2.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (Battery Regulation). Art 14: from 18 Aug 2024, the battery owner and third parties acting for them get read-only access to battery management system (BMS) data used to determine state of health (SoH) and expected lifetime, for EV, light-means-of-transport and stationary storage batteries. Art 77 and Annex XIII: a mandatory digital Battery Passport for EV and industrial batteries over 2 kWh from 18 Feb 2027, including dynamic SoH data available to 'persons with legitimate interest' (repairers, remanufacturers, second-life operators, and buyers/financiers in many interpretations). The Data Act adds access to vehicle telematics.
r2.dataset: SoH, capacity fade, internal resistance, cycle counts, fast-charge share and thermal history for every EV battery sold in the EU, read on demand with owner authorization and increasingly standardized through the passport. The outcome labels come when the same data is joined to used-EV auction and transaction prices, lease returns, warranty claims, and second-life sale prices. The question is how the market actually prices SoH and what the degradation curve looks like for each chemistry, pack and usage pattern, and a cross-OEM view of that does not exist.
r2.current_users: SoH testing and certificates: Aviloo (Austria), Volytica, Dekra, TUV, Generational/Recurrent (US). Battery analytics: Twaice, Elysia (Fortescue), Accure. Passport platforms: Circulor, Everledger (collapsed), Spherity, Siemens. OEM pilots: Kia, BMW, VW. Residual-value forecasting: Autovista/Glass's, Indicata, Cap HPI. Nobody clearly uses the data to take the residual-value risk itself; some pilots with lessors exist. This space is crowded on analytics, so score it on the risk-taking angle only.
r2.ml_unlock: A cross-OEM degradation and price model that predicts the SoH and the market value of a specific pack 3-5 years out. Uses: (a) residual-value guarantees and insurance sold to leasing companies and captive finance arms, which today load big risk premiums onto EV residuals and so make EV leases expensive; (b) lending against used EVs and second-life batteries; (c) buying EVs at lease end and arbitraging mispriced packs (cars priced by age and mileage, but with good batteries).
r2.path_to_1B: European EV leasing is now a majority of new BEV registrations. Collapsing EV residuals (2023-25) cost lessors billions; for example, Hertz and lessors such as Ayvens/ALD took large write-downs (from memory, not checked against a source). The EU fleet/leasing book runs to hundreds of billions of euros. A residual-value insurer or MGA charging 1-3% of vehicle value on tens of billions of insured value implies hundreds of millions of dollars in premium. Adding a used-EV trading arm puts a $1B+ outcome in reach.
r2.why_now: BMS access has been in force since Aug 2024 and the passport becomes mandatory in Feb 2027, so the data becomes broadly available in 2027-28, just as the first big wave of EU EV leases (2022-24) comes back to market. Lessors are actively looking for better residual tools after recent losses. The risks: OEMs may lock down passport dynamic data behind 'legitimate interest' gatekeeping, and the incumbents Aviloo and Autovista could add risk-bearing products.
r2.verified: Searched: Battery Passport pilots (Kia cell-level trial, Oct 2025). From memory: the Art 14 BMS access date (Aug 2024), the Feb 2027 passport date, the legitimate-interest access tier, the competitor list, and the lessor write-downs.

r2.name: Charger-reliability ground truth (EU AFIR mandated real-time status and price feeds)
r2.jurisdiction: EU (plus UK Public Charge Point Regulations 2023, with similar open data and 99% uptime mandates for rapid chargers)
r2.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 (AFIR) Art 20, with Delegated Regulation 2025/1754-ish (exact number not checked). Operators of publicly accessible chargers must make static data and dynamic data (operational status, availability, ad hoc price) available free of charge through national access points (NAPs), with dynamic-data duties phased in during 2025. The UK Public Charge Point Regulations 2023 require open data, 99% rapid-charger reliability reporting, and price transparency.
r2.dataset: A public, near-real-time feed of status (available, occupied, out of order) and ad hoc price for every public charge point in the EU, roughly 900k-1M points, through each country's NAP (NDW in the Netherlands, Mobilithek in Germany, data.gouv.fr in France). Logged over time, it yields labels: downtime and failure events per charger, per hardware model, per operator and per site, utilization proxies (occupied time), and price-elasticity experiments across operators. No one company owns this panel. Every operator sees only its own chargers.
r2.current_users: Eco-Movement (NL, global charge-point data aggregator, sells to OEMs and navigation apps). Paren (US, $3M seed, reliability and utilization data, mostly US). ChargerHelp (US, field reliability). Spirii and other CPO platforms handle AFIR compliance. Navigation apps and Google/Apple ingest the static data. Reliability analytics already exists, so a pure data-and-analytics play is crowded and small.
r2.ml_unlock: Hardware- and site-level failure and utilization models: predict which charger models fail, which sites will hit utilization X, and which price wins share. Use them to (a) underwrite uptime warranties or availability insurance for CPOs and hardware makers; (b) value and finance charging sites (project finance and charging-asset ABS) on the basis of observed utilization; (c) acquire underperforming sites from distressed CPOs and fix them (a roll-up).
r2.path_to_1B: EU public charging capex is roughly EUR 10-20B a year through 2030 (from memory, not checked against a source), and large charging-infrastructure financings are happening (Ionity, Electra, Fastned, Allego distress). A data-only business is likely capped below $200M a year, which fails the filter. The $1B path needs balance-sheet use: a site-acquisition and financing vehicle, or an insurer of charger availability. That is plausible but competes with infrastructure funds that will license the same data.
r2.why_now: The AFIR dynamic-data obligations went live in 2025, so the panel only now exists at scale. The CPO industry is consolidating and several operators are distressed (Allego delisted, many small CPOs failing), so assets are cheap to buy.
r2.verified: Searched: AFIR Art 20 dynamic data via NAPs (Spirii docs, Nationale Leitstelle, NDW 2025 implementing regulation); Paren and Eco-Movement exist. From memory: the UK 99% rule, charger counts, capex figures, and the delegated act number.

r2.name: Metered retrofit/heat-pump performance underwriter (UK smart meter DCC, Green Button, Smart Meter Texas, Australia CDR energy)
r2.jurisdiction: UK (DCC smart meter network), US (Green Button / Smart Meter Texas), Australia (Consumer Data Right, energy sector)
r2.legal_basis: UK Smart Energy Code: with consumer consent, licensed 'Other Users' can read half-hourly consumption from the DCC. US: Green Button Connect is mandated by some PUCs (California, Texas through Smart Meter Texas under PUCT rules). Australia: the Consumer Data Right rules for energy require retailers to share data with accredited recipients.
r2.dataset: Per-household interval consumption, about 36M UK smart meters (most of them SMETS2 on the DCC), plus Texas ERCOT-area meters. Before/after interval data around a retrofit, heat-pump install or solar/battery install is the outcome label: realized savings and realized peak-load shift, measured by the meter rather than modelled from EPC assessments.
r2.current_users: Octopus Energy (Kraken) has much of this internally. n3rgy, Hildebrand Glow and Loop (UK access providers). Recurve and OpenEEmeter (US, meter-based savings for pay-for-performance programs). Carbon Re, Kraken Flex and Axle Energy (flexibility). Partly occupied, and Octopus is a strong incumbent.
r2.ml_unlock: A counterfactual savings model trained on millions of before/after installs. It predicts the realized savings and flexibility value of a specific measure in a specific home, so the company can underwrite performance guarantees, fund heat pumps or retrofits through savings-share or green mortgages (repaid out of metered savings), and aggregate the homes into flexibility contracts.
r2.path_to_1B: The UK needs about GBP 250B+ of home decarbonization (from memory, not checked against a source), and the Warm Homes Plan is about GBP 13B of public money. The financing gap is the bottleneck: lenders cannot price retrofit savings. A lender/guarantor with a metered-savings edge could finance billions, and green mortgage partnerships widen the reach. Execution and policy risk are high, and outcomes are slow (12+ months of data after each install).
r2.why_now: SMETS2 rollout is mostly complete, the Warm Homes Plan is funding installs, heat-pump volumes are rising under the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, and market-wide half-hourly settlement (MHHS) goes live in 2025-27, which makes half-hourly data standard.
r2.verified: No searches spent on this candidate; all of it is from memory. Treat the regime details and market figures as unconfirmed until checked.

r2.jurisdiction: US, Australia, EU

r2.name: PAGA notice + settlement corpus -> wage-and-hour liability underwriting MGA (EPLI with wage/hour cover)
r2.jurisdiction: California (expandable: NY/NJ/WA wage-theft dockets, DOL WHD enforcement data nationally)
r2.legal_basis: Cal. Labor Code 2699(l) (PAGA): every PAGA claim notice must be filed with the LWDA before suit, and every proposed PAGA settlement (plus judgments) must be submitted to LWDA; LWDA publishes notices and settlement filings online. 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288/SB 92) kept filing duties and added cure/penalty-cap mechanics, and LWDA has been doing 2026 rulemaking on PAGA procedures. Federal complement: DOL WHD compliance-action data (back wages, CMPs by employer) is public.
r2.dataset: Roughly 7,000-9,000 PAGA notices/yr since 2016 (~80k+ total) as PDFs naming employer, alleged violations (meal/rest, OT, wage statements, misclassification), counsel; settlement submissions with gross amounts, PAGA allocation, class size, attorney fees. Searchable LWDA portal, scrapeable; needs OCR+entity resolution. Join with WHD enforcement CSVs, posted pay ranges (CA SB 1162) and EDD/WARN data for employer features.
r2.current_users: Plaintiff firms mine it informally; CABIA (business lobby) and Ankura did aggregate analyses; Lex Machina/Docket Alarm/Trellis cover court dockets but not the LWDA settlement corpus as a pricing dataset. EPLI carriers (Chubb, AIG, Beazley) generally exclude wage-and-hour or sublimit it, and price it crudely. No known funded startup underwriting wage-and-hour risk off this data (not verified exhaustively).
r2.ml_unlock: Labeled outcome dataset (notice -> did it settle, for how much, per-employee) lets a model price expected wage-and-hour loss per employer from public features (industry, headcount, pay structure, prior notices, counsel). Forward-looking: predict which employers will get a PAGA notice within 12 months. That is the missing actuarial base for an insurable product that carriers currently exclude.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers: CA employers (wage-and-hour class+PAGA settlements run multi-billion $/yr in CA; top-10 wage/hour settlements nationally were ~$0.5-0.7B/yr per Seyfarth reports, from memory). US EPLI premium ~$2.5-3B (from memory). Become an MGA writing wage-and-hour defense+indemnity cover backed by reinsurers, then expand to NY/NJ/IL wage-theft regimes and multistate employers. Secondary revenue: risk scores sold to PEOs (who carry this risk across hundreds of thousands of SMB worksite employees) and M&A diligence. $1B path = MGA with $300-500M GWP or PEO/insurer embedded pricing; adverse-selection and moral-hazard risk is real.
r2.why_now: 2024 PAGA reform changed penalty math (caps for employers who cure), so old pricing heuristics broke and a fresh model has an edge; pay transparency laws now give public pay-structure features per employer; LLMs make OCR/extraction of ~100k messy PDF notices and settlements cheap.
r2.verified: Verified by search: LWDA PAGA filing portal exists and analyses of PAGA settlement filings have been done (Ankura, CABIA); LWDA 2026 rulemaking comments exist. From memory: filing volumes, settlement-submission requirement since 2016, EPLI market size, absence of a startup MGA on this.

r2.name: EU pay-gap reports -> equal-pay claims origination and litigation funding
r2.jurisdiction: EU-27 (plus UK Equality Act equal-pay claims and UK gender pay gap reporting)
r2.legal_basis: Directive (EU) 2023/970 (transposition deadline 7 June 2026; most member states missed it, several in progress): employers 150+ must publish gender pay gap reports (first reports 2027 for 150+/250+), mandatory joint pay assessment where unexplained gap >=5%, worker right to request pay info, burden of proof shifted to employer, no caps on compensation, representative actions by equality bodies/unions. UK: Equality Act 2010 gender pay gap regs publish ~10k employer reports/yr since 2017.
r2.dataset: UK: ~10.5k employers/yr x 8 years of quartile pay, mean/median gap, bonus gap (gender-pay-gap.service.gov.uk, CSV). EU: from 2027 national registries of employer gap reports by category of worker; job-posting pay ranges mandated by directive. Outcomes: UK employment tribunal decisions are public (gov.uk ET decisions DB), plus big equal-pay group claims (Asda, Tesco, Next, Birmingham council ~GBP1B+).
r2.current_users: Compliance side is crowded: Trusaic, Syndio, Figures (FR), Ravio, beqom/PayAnalytics, Gapsquare (XpertHR), Mercer, Payfit. Plaintiff side: UK firms Leigh Day, Harcus Parker, Fieldfisher with litigation funders funding supermarket equal-pay claims; nobody known running ML claim-origination across EU registries.
r2.ml_unlock: Score every reporting employer for expected recoverable equal-pay liability: combine published gap structure, sector job evaluation norms, posting ranges, workforce composition and tribunal outcome history to predict which employers have large unexplained gaps that will fail a joint pay assessment and how much a group claim would recover. The company takes a position by funding/originating group claims (or selling the score to employers/insurers/acquirers).
r2.path_to_1B: UK equal-pay group claims alone have aggregate exposure in the multi-billions GBP (Asda claim estimates ~GBP1.2B; Birmingham ~GBP1B+, from memory). EU directive removes caps and shifts burden across 27 countries. A litigation-finance vehicle with a data-driven origination edge (like Burford's model, ~$500M+ revenue) could reach $1B valuation; flip side, sell 'pay-liability score' to insurers (EPLI/W&I for M&A) and acquirers. Risks: slow litigation cycles, regulatory hostility to third-party funding in EU, first EU data only 2027-28.
r2.why_now: Directive deadline passed June 2026; first mandatory reports and joint pay assessments land 2027-2028; uncapped compensation + burden reversal create a new liability class before anyone has priced it.
r2.verified: Verified by search: transposition deadline passed with most member states late (Littler/Trusaic monitors). From memory: UK data volumes, specific claim sizes, competitor list on compliance side.

r2.name: H-1B/PERM outcome model -> immigration petition underwriting (approval-guaranteed filing / fee insurance) under weighted lottery + $100k fee regime
r2.jurisdiction: United States
r2.legal_basis: INA/20 CFR 655 and 656: DOL OFLC publishes every LCA (employer, title, SOC, worksite, wage level, offered wage) and every PERM case with status (certified/denied/withdrawn) and prevailing wage determinations; USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub publishes approvals/denials/RFEs per employer. DHS final rule (Dec 2025) made FY2027 H-1B cap selection wage-level weighted; Sept 2025 proclamation imposed a $100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions.
r2.dataset: ~600-800k LCAs/yr, ~100k+ PERM cases/yr with outcomes, prevailing wage determinations, USCIS employer-level approval/denial counts; quarterly Excel files from OFLC, 2001-present. Outcome labels: PERM certified vs denied, PWD levels, H-1B approvals/denials/RFEs per employer.
r2.current_users: Heavily mined: Levels.fyi, h1bdata.info, MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader, Revelio Labs, Lightcast, Pave/Carta for comp; immigration platforms Boundless, Alma, Deel/Remote immigration, Envoy Global, Lawfully use it for case-status and employer analytics. Comp angle is fully commoditized.
r2.ml_unlock: Under wage-weighted selection plus a $100k fee, each petition is a priced bet: model selection odds by wage level, RFE/denial probability from title/SOC/wage/employer history, and PERM audit/denial risk. Product: fixed-price filing with refund/insurance if denied, or financing of the $100k fee against predicted approval and retention.
r2.path_to_1B: Employers spend several $B/yr on US business immigration legal fees (Fragomen alone ~$1B+ revenue, from memory). Path: tech-enabled immigration firm/insurer that prices outcome risk better than law firms. But the $100k fee and policy volatility shrink H-1B volume, data edge is thin because everyone has the same OFLC files, and outcomes are driven by politics more than features. Plausible $1B only as a broad immigration platform, which already has funded players.
r2.why_now: First weighted lottery (FY2027, run March 2026) and $100k fee created brand-new pricing uncertainty for every employer.
r2.verified: Verified by search: weighted selection final rule and $100k fee applied to FY2027 cycle. From memory: data volumes, competitor list, Fragomen revenue.

r2.name: Public wage disclosures as labels for an income-estimation bureau (Work Number alternative for lenders)
r2.jurisdiction: US (pay-range laws in CO, CA, WA, NY, IL, MD, MN, VT, MA, NJ, DC etc.; LCA wages; public-sector salary databases)
r2.legal_basis: State pay transparency statutes (e.g. CO Equal Pay for Equal Work Act 2021, CA SB 1162, NY Labor Law 194-b, WA RCW 49.58.110, IL EPA amendments 2025, MA 2025) force salary ranges into job postings; DOL LCA disclosure gives individual offered wages; state public-records laws make public-employee pay public (~20M public workers).

r2.legal_basis: Norway Ligningsloven/skatteforvaltningsloven skattelister (income, wealth, tax per citizen; searches logged and visible to the searched person since 2014, bulk access only to press); Sweden offentlighetsprincipen (taxeringskalender, Ratsit/Mrkoll); Finland annual public tax data release to media; IRS Form 990 Schedule J officer comp; US state pay-range posting laws.
