r2.name: Brazil farm-level agri-credit underwriter/lender built on SICOR polygons + CAR + PRODES/DETER + IBAMA embargoes + rural judicial-recovery filings
r2.jurisdiction: Brazil
r2.legal_basis: BCB/CMN rules (e.g. Res. 4,427/2015 and successors) require every subsidized rural credit operation to be registered in SICOR with the georeferenced polygon (gleba) of the financed area. BCB publishes SICOR operation-level open data. The Forest Code (Lei 12.651/2012) makes CAR self-declared property polygons public. INPE publishes PRODES/DETER deforestation by law and mandate. IBAMA embargo lists are public. Court filings for producer recuperação judicial (now allowed for individual producers since Lei 14.112/2020) are public and give the default labels.
r2.dataset: SICOR: millions of rural credit contracts per year (Plano Safra is about R$500B+/yr) with crop, area, amount, rate, program, municipality and gleba coordinates (BCB dadosabertos, DEROP). CAR: about 7M property polygons (SICAR download). PRODES/DETER rasters and alerts (TerraBrasilis). IBAMA embargo shapefiles. CPR (cédula de produto rural) registrations at B3/CERC registries (aggregate stats). RJ/bankruptcy filings scraped from state courts (TJMT, TJGO and others) as outcome labels. Everything joins on space plus CPF/CNPJ.
r2.current_users: MapBiomas 'Monitor do Crédito Rural' (NGO) already crosses SICOR glebas with deforestation. Agri-fintechs: Traive (AI credit scoring for agro), Agrolend (bank license), Terramagna, Tarken, Agrotools/Serasa Experian Agro score, Bayer/Orbia credit, plus Brazilian banks' in-house teams. Satellite-ESG players: Satelligence, Agrosatélite, Trase. The data is known. What does not exist is a model trained on public credit history + land/deforestation compliance + RJ default outcomes that is used to take balance-sheet risk.
r2.ml_unlock: Parcel-level probability of default and probability of compliance block (embargo, CAR overlap, EUDR/soy-moratorium exclusion), learned from SICOR history, satellite yield proxies and RJ labels. Use it to originate and securitize CPRs and Fiagro/CRA paper at better pricing than incumbents, and to sell an 'EUDR-clean, credit-scored' parcel feed to traders (Cargill, Bunge, ADM, Amaggi) and to banks.
r2.path_to_1B: Brazil agri credit needs about R$1T+/yr. Private CPR stock is above R$400B (B3/CERC stats, from memory) and grew fast after the 2019-2021 CPR reforms. The 2024-26 wave of producer RJ filings has made banks pull back, which opens a credit gap. A data-advantaged lender/securitizer taking 1-2% of CPR origination (R$5-10B book) at a 3-4% net spread is enough for $1B+ equity value. The model is 'Nubank for soy/cattle farms', with the trader compliance feed as a second revenue line.
r2.why_now: EUDR applies from Dec 2026 for large operators after the second delay and the 2025 simplification. Brazil is classified standard risk, so traders need parcel-level proof. The rural RJ surge (2024-26) produces the first large set of default labels. Bank credit is retreating. SICOR polygon data has become usable with modern geospatial ML.
r2.verified: Searched: EUDR was delayed again with a 2026 simplification package (Stibbe, CMS, VinciWorks). BCB SICOR open data under DEROP exists, MapBiomas runs a 2025 Rural Credit Monitor crossing it with deforestation, and Res. 4427/2015 is on BCB. From memory and not verified: the exact SICOR polygon fields in open data (they may be partly aggregated or restricted), CPR stock figures, competitors' funding amounts, and the RJ statistics.

r2.name: EUTL installation-level compliance-position model for trading EUAs and UK/Swiss allowances (and later CBAM certificates)
r2.jurisdiction: EU (plus UK ETS, Switzerland; CBAM certificates from 2027)
r2.legal_basis: The EU ETS Directive 2003/87/EC and the Union Registry Regulation require the public EU Transaction Log (EUTL) to publish, per installation and aircraft operator, the verified emissions, free allocation, surrendered units and compliance status every year. Transaction-level transfers between accounts are published with a multi-year lag (about 3 years, from memory).
r2.dataset: About 10k-12k stationary installations plus aircraft and maritime operators. Annual verified emissions, free allocation, surrenders and compliance codes since 2005. Historical account-to-account transfers, which show who hedges, who is short and which intermediaries hold positions. Available as EUTL web downloads and cleaned versions such as EUETS.info.
r2.current_users: Heavily mined: Veyt (ex-Refinitiv carbon), ICIS, BloombergNEF, ClearBlue Markets, Vertis, Redshaw, Energy Aspects, trading desks of utilities, banks and hedge funds, and academic EUETS.info. Fundamental modelling with ML on top of EUTL is standard practice at these firms.
r2.ml_unlock: Nowcast each installation's emissions (from satellite NO2/CO2 data, power generation, production indices) and its implied short or long position before the April 30 verified-emissions release. Infer hedging behaviour from the lagged transfer graph. Trade the release and the surrender season, and later CBAM certificate demand from importers.
r2.path_to_1B: EU carbon is about €700-900B/yr in traded notional and the largest carbon market. Edge would be monetized through a prop or quant fund, not data sales, because the data-vendor niche is small and crowded. That is a hedge-fund path, so YC fit and defensibility are weak.
r2.why_now: ETS2 (buildings and transport) starts 2027-28. Maritime is phased in for 2024-26. Free allocation phases down as CBAM's definitive period begins (2026), which adds new data-poor participants. Even so, the core dataset is 20 years old and well understood.
r2.verified: From memory: the EUTL disclosure rules, the transfer lag and market size. Not searched, to save budget. The competitor list is from memory and high-confidence.

r2.name: Carbon-credit delivery and reversal underwriter using registry PDDs, monitoring reports and issuance histories
r2.jurisdiction: Global (Verra VCS, Gold Standard, CDM/Article 6.4, ACR, CAR, Puro, Isometric)
r2.legal_basis: Registry program rules (not statute) require the PDD, validation and verification reports, monitoring reports and VVB findings to be public. Issuances, retirements and buffer contributions and cancellations are public in the registries. CDM documents are public under UNFCCC rules.
r2.dataset: About 4k+ Verra and 3k+ Gold Standard projects and about 8k CDM projects, each with ex-ante projected credits and actual issuance over time. That gives a built-in label for delivery shortfall, plus reversal and buffer-cancellation events, VVB corrective action requests and methodology changes. Access is by registry scraping (PDFs).
r2.current_users: Crowded. Sylvera (raised about $96M), BeZero (ratings, about $50M+), Calyx Global, Renoster, Pachama, MSCI Carbon Markets (ex-Trove), Kita (delivery-risk insurance with Chaucer/Lloyd's, about $29M round), Oka, Howden carbon insurance, CarbonPlan (open-source analysis). Several of them already use ML on these documents and on satellite data.
r2.ml_unlock: Predict the ratio of issued to projected credits and the probability of reversal or invalidation from PDD text, developer history, VVB identity and geospatial risk. Use it to price forward offtakes, prepay finance and delivery insurance.
r2.path_to_1B: The voluntary carbon market is only about $0.5-1B/yr retired value after the 2023-24 integrity crash. A $1B path depends on Article 6, CORSIA Phase 1 and CRCF compliance demand growing, and incumbents already hold the rating and insurance positions.
r2.why_now: CORSIA Phase 1 (2024-26) demand, Article 6.4 issuances and ICVCM CCP labels create new compliance buyers. Even so, the field is saturated.
r2.verified: Searched: Kita's carbon delivery insurance and its Chaucer partnership plus funding (fintech.global, decarbonfuse). Other funding figures are from memory.

r2.name: Nordic timberland pricing and lending engine on public stand-level forest data plus official land-sale price registers
r2.jurisdiction: Finland (primary), Sweden, Norway
r2.legal_basis: Finland's Forest Information Act (amended 2018-19) makes Finnish Forest Centre (Metsäkeskus) stand-level data from laser scanning and inventories open data, covering species, volume and age per stand. Real-estate purchase price registers (Maanmittauslaitos in Finland, Lantmäteriet in Sweden) record every forest property sale price by law. National Forest Inventories are public statistics. Clearcut notifications are mandatory and public (Finland's forest use declarations, Swedish Skogsstyrelsen avverkningsanmälan).
r2.dataset: Open stand polygons for about 20M ha of Finnish private forest, the full history of transaction prices (labels), harvest notifications as cash-flow labels, and plot-level NFI. Sweden has open felling notifications and laser-derived forest maps.
r2.current_users: Forest management and valuation tools (Metsään.fi, Silvia, Treemetrics, Collective Crunch, Arbonaut, Simosol), US analogs NCX and Pachama for carbon, and Nordic forest brokers (OP, Metsäliitto). Little evidence of an ML-driven buyer or lender using the price register.
r2.ml_unlock: Automated valuation of any forest parcel from open stand data, with predicted harvest cash flows and price. Use it to run an iBuyer or instant-mortgage product for fragmented family forest holdings, or a timberland fund that buys mispriced parcels.
r2.path_to_1B: Finnish private forest sales are about €1-2B/yr and Sweden's are larger (about SEK 20B+/yr, from memory). A Nordic-only product struggles to reach $1B. It needs expansion to the US (FIA plus county deed records) and the Baltics, or to become a balance-sheet timberland investor. Market risk is high.
r2.why_now: Open laser-scan data now covers multiple scanning cycles, so growth can be measured. Generational transfer of family forests and EU nature-restoration rules add pressure on valuation.
r2.verified: From memory only, with no search budget spent: the Finnish open forest data law and the price-register availability. Treat as unverified.

r2.name: EUDR compliance network (DDS reference-number graph plus geolocation)
r2.jurisdiction: EU
r2.legal_basis: EUDR (Reg. 2023/1115, amended 2024 and 2025) requires due diligence statements with plot geolocation filed in the EU Information System (TRACES). The statements are NOT public. Only country benchmarking and aggregate enforcement data are published.
r2.dataset: No public plot-level DDS data. Public inputs are only third-party layers (GFW, JRC forest map, PRODES, CAR).
r2.current_users: Very crowded: osapiens (raised large rounds, about $120M), Satelligence, Meridia, Koltiva, Preferred by Nature, TrusTrace, Sourcemap, Global Forest Watch Pro, Agrotools, plus SAP/Ecovadis add-ons.
r2.ml_unlock: Deforestation-risk scoring per plot. This is commodity work now and has no proprietary label advantage.
r2.path_to_1B: This is a compliance SaaS race with dozens of funded players, and the application date has been delayed twice and simplified. There is no data moat because the forced disclosure goes to regulators, not the public. Use EUDR only as a demand driver for candidate 1.
r2.why_now: Large operators apply from Dec 2026 and small operators in 2027, but the scope has been watered down.
r2.verified: Searched: the second delay and the 2025-26 simplification (Bird & Bird, CMS, Stibbe, VinciWorks, lexgo). That DDS is not public is from memory.

r2.name: India IBC/NCLT + SARFAESI auction outcomes: ML recovery pricing for stressed Indian credit (a tech-enabled ARC or special-situations buyer)
r2.jurisdiction: India
r2.legal_basis: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016. IBBI regulations require the outcome of every corporate insolvency (CIRP) and liquidation to be disclosed publicly: admitted claims, liquidation value and fair value (from mandatory dual valuations), plan realisation, timelines, and the NCLT/NCLAT orders. Separately, the SARFAESI Act 2002 and the Security Interest Enforcement Rules force banks to publish every secured-asset auction notice (newspaper plus e-auction portal: IBAPI/BAANKNET) with reserve price, and then the result. Companies Act 2013 forces every private company to file audited financials and charges on MCA21.
r2.dataset: About 8,000+ CIRPs admitted since 2016, each with a claims, valuation and outcome record (IBBI quarterly newsletters plus the case database). Tens of thousands of NCLT orders as PDFs. SARFAESI e-auction notices on IBAPI/BAANKNET (hundreds of thousands of property listings with reserve price, often re-listed at a lower reserve after a failed auction, which is an implicit outcome label). MCA21 financials and charge registers for about 1.8M active companies (Tofler/Probe42 resell them). The labels are realised recovery as a % of claims or of liquidation value, time to resolution, and failed-auction sequences. All of it is public. Joining it requires scraping NCLT PDFs and matching entities through CIN.
r2.current_users: Credit-data aggregators (Probe42, Tofler, CredHive, Zauba, Signzy) sell raw MCA data for KYC and credit checks. Rating agencies (CARE, CRISIL, ICRA) publish aggregate IBC recovery studies. ARCs (Edelweiss ARC, Arcil, the government-backed NARCL, plus Kotak, Cerberus and Bain-backed vehicles) price NPL portfolios mostly from bank data rooms and in-house legal teams. insolvencytracker.in tracks cases. I found no funded startup that sells or trades on an ML recovery model trained on the full IBC + SARFAESI outcome corpus. That is unverified beyond one search.
r2.ml_unlock: A model that, for any stressed borrower or collateral, predicts realised recovery %, time-to-cash and probability of liquidation versus resolution. It would be trained on every IBC and SARFAESI outcome, joined to the debtor's MCA financials, charge stack, court history and collateral location and type. No single bank or ARC sees more than its own book. The model also prices a single SARFAESI auction property: whether it will clear at reserve, and at what discount after N failures.
r2.path_to_1B: Indian banks plus NBFCs carry gross NPAs of roughly Rs 4-5 lakh crore and have written off Rs 10+ lakh crore over the past decade. IBC haircuts are about 67% (Business Standard, Nov 2025, from IBBI data to Sep 2025). Recovery from large cases is about 33% of claims. The software layer (pricing tool for ARCs, banks and AIFs) is maybe $50-100M ARR. That fails the size filter on its own. The $1B path is to take the risk: become (or partner with) an RBI-licensed ARC or a Category-II AIF special-situations fund that buys NPL tranches and SARFAESI properties where the model says the discount is mispriced. A $1-2B AUM vehicle earning 20%+ IRR plus a management fee, combined with a data business, supports a $1B+ valuation. The license requirement (ARC net-owned funds of Rs 300 crore) is a moat but is heavy for a YC-stage team. Start as the analytics provider and co-investor.
r2.why_now: IBC is now about 9 years old, so there are enough closed cases to supply labels (a long tail of resolutions and liquidations finished in 2022-2025). NARCL/IDRCL and the 2024-25 BAANKNET centralised e-auction portal put SARFAESI listings in one structured place. RBI's 2021-22 framework widened ARC and secondary-loan-market participation (the secondary loan market platform). LLMs can now extract structured fields from Hindi/English NCLT orders and valuation summaries cheaply.
r2.verified: Searched: IBC haircut of about 67% and recovery for large cases of about 33% of FC claims (Business Standard, Nov 2025; insolvencytracker, Aug 2025). From memory (unverified): CIRP count, the BAANKNET launch, the NPA/write-off figures, the ARC NOF requirement, and the absence of a direct ML competitor.

r2.name: Korea jeonse/rent mandatory reporting + MOLIT sale prices + registry: ML jeonse-deposit default underwriting
r2.jurisdiction: South Korea
r2.legal_basis: Real Estate Transaction Reporting Act. Sales must be reported to MOLIT within 30 days, and the price is published per unit (floor, size, date). The 2021 amendment (전월세 신고제) requires every residential lease above KRW 60M deposit or KRW 300k/month (in covered areas) to be reported within 30 days. The grace period ended 1 June 2025, after which non-reporting is fined. MOLIT publishes the reported jeonse/monthly-rent deposit and rent per unit on rt.molit.go.kr and the public data portal. Every property's registry (등기부등본: mortgages, seizures, owner changes) is public for a small fee via IROS. Court auction outcomes (courtauction.go.kr) give the default labels.
r2.dataset: Every apartment and villa sale price since 2006, and every reported lease deposit since 2021 (now near-complete for covered leases after June 2025 enforcement). These are millions of records per year, with API access via data.go.kr. Registry liens and seizures come from per-property fetches. Labels come from three sources: court and KAMCO Onbid auctions with winning bids; HUG's own subrogation (대위변제) events, published in aggregate; and the joint pattern where a deposit exceeds the later sale or auction value (깡통전세). The sub-signal is per-landlord portfolios (serial landlords behind the 2022-23 jeonse fraud wave), which you can reconstruct from registry ownership.
r2.current_users: Hogangnono (acquired by Zigbang), Zigbang, Naver Real Estate, KB Real Estate, Asil and Dabang show jeonse ratios. The government's 안심전세 app and HUG risk checks provide basic jeonse-ratio and lien warnings. Startups such as 집품 (zippoom) and 'safehomes' publish tenant guidance. HUG, SGI Seoul Guarantee and HF (Korea Housing Finance Corp) underwrite deposit-return guarantees with rule-based limits (e.g., the 126% → 90% LTV-style caps). Consumer-facing jeonse-ratio display is therefore commoditised. What I did not find is a private underwriter or lender pricing guarantee risk per unit and per landlord with ML.
r2.ml_unlock: A per-unit, per-landlord probability that a jeonse deposit will not be returned at lease end. It would be trained on sale-price paths, lease-deposit paths, landlord multi-property leverage reconstructed from the registry, building type (villas and officetels are worst), and auction recovery. Uses: (a) price deposit-return guarantees by risk instead of with flat caps; (b) bridge-lend to tenants or landlords against deposits (전세대출 refinancing); (c) let investors buy discounted deposit claims (subrogated receivables) from HUG and recover them through auction.
r2.path_to_1B: The jeonse deposit stock is estimated at roughly KRW 800-1,000 trillion (about $600-700B). HUG paid out on the order of KRW 3-4 trillion per year in deposit subrogation at the 2023-24 peak, and still about KRW 1 trillion+ per half-year in 2025 (Segye, Jul 2025). HUG ran losses, and in 2025 it cut guarantee coverage, which leaves underserved tenants. Who pays: tenants and landlords for guarantee premia, banks for jeonse-loan risk models, and HUG/SGI and the debt buyers of subrogated claims (HUG holds trillions of KRW of claims to recover). $1B path: become a licensed or fronted guarantee/insurance MGA using a carrier's paper (e.g., with SGI or a foreign insurer), plus a fund that buys HUG's subrogated deposit receivables. The barrier is Korean regulatory and licensing. A foreign founder without Korean partners is a big gap.
r2.why_now: Lease reporting only became enforced in June 2025, so for the first time there is a near-complete public lease-deposit series per unit. The fraud wave (2022-24) created labels. HUG is retreating (stricter guarantee ratio, LTV cut to 90%), which opens room for risk-priced private capacity. Policy debate about phasing out jeonse also creates refinancing demand.
r2.verified: Searched: lease-reporting grace period ended June 2025 with fines (Newsis, Etoday). HUG subrogation is still KRW 1T+ scale and HUG tightened guarantees (Segye, Daum, NewsTomato). From memory: the deposit-stock estimate, the Hogangnono/Zigbang landscape, and the absence of a private ML underwriter.

r2.name: India RERA quarterly progress filings: ML project-completion risk for construction finance, homebuyer loans and completion guarantees
r2.jurisdiction: India (state RERAs: MahaRERA, UP-RERA, HRERA, K-RERA, TNRERA, etc.)
r2.legal_basis: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016. Every project above 500 sq m or 8 units must register before marketing. It must publish approvals, land title, encumbrances, layout, unit inventory, a 70% escrow requirement, and quarterly progress reports (QPRs) with construction stage %, units sold and money collected/withdrawn. It must also publish CA/engineer certificates, extension requests, complaints and penalty orders. All of this is public per project on the state portals. A unified RERA portal launched in 2025.
r2.dataset: About 150k+ registered projects across states (MahaRERA alone has about 50k). Each has quarterly time series of construction progress, sales and escrow withdrawals, plus completion-date revisions and extensions. Complaint and order texts are attached. The $1B path: (a) a real-estate credit/AIF platform that lends last-mile and structured construction finance using the model, as SWAMIH does at Rs 15k+ crore; or (b) a completion-guarantee/surety MGA (IRDAI allowed surety bonds in 2022) priced on RERA data, then extend to all RERA-like regimes. Also sell the signal to insurer-equity investors and to reinsurers for casualty treaty pricing. Comparable: Enstar-scale run-off consolidators are worth $3-6B.

r2.name: Private-credit loan marks graph from BDC Schedules of Investments plus N-PORT: an independent pricing/default model used to buy secondaries, provide NAV/back-leverage, or rate private loans for insurers

BDCs and registered funds must list every portfolio investment (borrower, spread, maturity, cost, fair value) each quarter in 10-Q/10-K. Form N-PORT (Rule 30b1-9) requires position-level holdings with fair value and Level 1/2/3 classification, public quarterly with a 60-day lag. Monthly public N-PORT was adopted in 2024, compliance was later pushed out, and in Feb 2026 the SEC proposed further N-PORT amendments, so monthly public frequency is uncertain.

Available on EDGAR (XBRL schedule-of-investments tagging is improving; edgartools parses BDC filings).

Octus (formerly Reorg) publishes 'one in five BDC loans marked below 90 falls into nonaccrual within 15 months', Solve does quarterly BDC mark-up/mark-down analysis, and Preqin, PitchBook LCD, KBRA DLD, 9fin, Fitch and the Boston Fed (2026 working paper) also work here. PIMCO comments on BDC mark signals. So mark-dispersion data is already productized; differentiation would have to come from taking risk, not from the dataset.
r2.ml_unlock: Use cross-manager disagreement on the same loan, plus the trajectory of marks, PIK/non-accrual transitions and borrower text, to predict default and recovery 12-18 months ahead. Identify stale or optimistic marks across managers (First Brands/Tricolor-type surprises). Produce a 'true price' for every private loan that no single manager can compute.
r2.path_to_1B: Private credit is about $1.7-2T AUM, and insurers hold several hundred billion $ of private placements that need NAIC SVO / private letter ratings. A data product alone competes with Octus, Solve and KBRA. The $1B paths: (a) a private-credit secondaries/continuation buyer or NAV lender that uses the model to pick mispriced loans and portfolios; (b) an NRSRO-style private letter rating shop for insurers (KBRA/Egan-Jones grew on this; NAIC is now scrutinizing PLR quality, which opens a door for an evidence-based rater).
r2.why_now: In 2025-26 private credit is under stress (rising non-accruals and PIK, BDC discounts to NAV), regulators are looking hard at private letter ratings, and position-level N-PORT/BDC data now spans enough cycles to train on.
r2.verified: Searched and verified: Octus and Solve already sell BDC-mark analytics; there is a Boston Fed 2026 paper on the topic; the SEC proposed N-PORT amendments in Feb 2026. From memory: the size of the private credit market, insurer private-placement holdings, and the NAIC PLR scrutiny.

r2.current_users: Crowded. Clarus Financial Technology (SDRView, acquired by CME in 2023 per memory), Bloomberg, dealers' internal desks and hedge funds all mine it. Commodity swap prints are used by OPIS and Argus-adjacent analysts.

r2.name: ProZorro contractor-risk underwriter for Ukraine reconstruction (surety, bid and performance guarantees, receivables finance)
r2.jurisdiction: Ukraine (the same approach could later extend to Moldova, Georgia and Kazakhstan's goszakup, which run similar open e-procurement systems)
r2.legal_basis: The Law of Ukraine 'On Public Procurement' (No. 922-VIII, 2015, amended 2019) requires public procurement above set thresholds to run through the ProZorro e-system. Every bid, every participant, any disqualification, every complaint to the AMCU (Ukraine's competition authority), the contract, its amendments and its performance and termination reports are published as open data in the OCDS standard. Bid security is posted as e-guarantees through the system.
r2.dataset: About 10 years of complete tender records: millions of procedures, with every bidder's price, not only the winner's. It covers which bids were disqualified and why, AMCU complaint outcomes, contract amendments (price creep), termination and non-performance reports, and links between buyers and suppliers. It is available through the public API (public.api.openprocurement.org) and the OCDS bulk export, and joins to the EDR company register (directors and beneficial owners) and court registers (reyestr.court.gov.ua).
r2.current_users: DOZORRO (Transparency International Ukraine) runs ML risk indicators to flag violations. ProZorro's own automatic risk indicators are used by the State Audit Service. Bi.prozorro.org runs public analytics. YouControl and Opendatabot are large commercial company-intelligence firms that ingest ProZorro, as do many bid-alert SaaS tools. Each of these targets corruption risk or bid alerts. None that I know of uses the data to price contractor default or underwrite guarantees.
r2.ml_unlock: A model of contractor performance trained on labels: whether a contractor completed the contract, terminated it, raised the price through amendments, lost an AMCU complaint, or was disqualified. Features are bid behaviour (discount versus estimate, number of competitors, related-party bidding networks), firm financials from the EDR, and court cases. The prediction is the probability that a given contractor finishes a given reconstruction contract on time and on budget. With it you can issue surety and performance bonds and finance receivables for contractors that banks and Western sureties won't touch because they can't assess them.
r2.path_to_1B: The World Bank's RDNA4 (Feb 2025) estimated Ukraine's recovery needs at about $524B over 10 years. Donor and MDB money (the EU Ukraine Facility of EUR 50B, the EBRD, the World Bank, the URC process) requires guarantees and fiduciary controls. Surety premiums run 1-3% of contract value, so at $30-50B a year of contracts the guarantee and contractor-finance pool is roughly $1B a year in premium plus a receivables book. The most credible route is an MGA backed by MDB or DFC reinsurance (MIGA and DFC already back Ukraine war-risk programmes). Risk-scoring software sold to donors and IFIs is a secondary revenue line. Reaching $1B depends on reconstruction actually reaching scale and on the war ending or freezing.
r2.why_now: Reconstruction money is starting to flow through ProZorro (the DREAM ecosystem links it to reconstruction project tracking), and donors are demanding transparency. A decade of labelled performance data now exists, and Western insurers lack local underwriting capability.
r2.verified: Searched and confirmed: ProZorro and DOZORRO already run ML or automated risk indicators (OECD OPSI case; TI Ukraine blog; Cabinet of Ministers news on automatic risk signals) and EBRD published a 2025 review of ProZorro's economic impact. From memory, not verified: the RDNA4 figure of $524B, the EU Ukraine Facility at EUR 50B, the DREAM linkage, and that contract performance and termination data are complete enough to serve as labels (the termination-reason fields are known to be noisy).

r2.name: Dubai off-plan completion-risk engine for off-plan purchase finance and delivery insurance (DLD/RERA escrow data)
r2.jurisdiction: UAE (Dubai)
r2.legal_basis: Dubai Law 8/2007 on escrow accounts for real-estate development requires developers to put buyer payments into project escrow, and RERA tracks construction progress percentages to release funds. Law 13/2008 (the interim real-estate register, Oqood) requires every off-plan sale to be registered. Law 26/2007 requires every lease to be registered through Ejari. DLD publishes transactions, projects, rents and broker data on Dubai Pulse and its open-data portal.
r2.dataset: Every sale transaction, both off-plan and ready, with price, unit, project and date (roughly 180k+ a year at more than AED 700B in 2024, from memory). It also includes project registrations with developer, escrow agent, planned and actual completion dates and completion percentage, Ejari rental contracts that show realised yields, and project status, including cancelled or stalled projects that RERA has liquidated after the 2008-2011 crash.
r2.current_users: Property Monitor, DXBinteract (Bayut/Dubizzle), Reidin, Data Finder by Property Finder and Huspy (mortgage broker, $59M Series B) are users of the data. Most importantly, Oliva (joinoliva.com) markets itself with 'Underwrite before you commit' and already publishes developer-risk reviews and off-plan project scores built on this data, so the analytics layer is already contested. Banks barely lend on off-plan property.
r2.ml_unlock: A model of project delivery and price outcomes: the probability of delay, cancellation or a price drop at handover for each off-plan project and developer. It is trained on 15+ years of RERA progress curves, cancellations, developer history, escrow inflows (from Oqood registrations) and resale behaviour, and it lets you lend against off-plan installment plans or insure delivery.
r2.path_to_1B: Off-plan is roughly 55-65% of Dubai transaction value (memory), which is $60-100B a year of contracts paid in installments over 3-5 years with almost no bank finance. That means billions in installment receivables waiting to be financed. A balance-sheet lender or insurer could build a $10B+ book, but this is one emirate in a cyclical, crash-prone market, and the main risk sits with whoever holds the book.
r2.why_now: Record off-plan volumes in 2023-2026 and widespread fears of oversupply create demand for both finance and protection. The 2008-2011 cancellation history provides labels for a downturn.
r2.verified: Searched: Oliva (joinoliva.com) exists and offers developer and project underwriting reviews for Dubai off-plan, which is a direct competitor. From memory, not verified: that RERA completion percentages are bulk-downloadable on Dubai Pulse (I believe a projects dataset exists but did not confirm it has the progress history), the volume figures, and the off-plan share.

r2.name: Polish and Czech insolvency, enforcement and contract-register model for SME credit, claims trading and NPL pricing
r2.jurisdiction: Poland (KRZ and KRS), Czech Republic (Registr smluv, ISIR), Slovakia (CRZ)
r2.legal_basis: Poland's Act on the National Register of Indebted Persons (KRZ, live since 1 Dec 2021) makes public the full electronic files of restructuring and bankruptcy proceedings, plus debtors whose bailiff enforcement was discontinued as ineffective. Poland's KRS requires every company's annual financial statements to be filed electronically and made freely available. Czech Act 340/2015 says a public-body contract over CZK 50k takes effect only once its full text is published in the Registr smluv. Slovakia has had an equivalent rule since 2011. Czech ISIR is the public insolvency register.
r2.dataset: KRZ holds proceeding files, including creditor lists with claim amounts, restructuring arrangements, creditor voting outcomes and court decisions. Together with KRS financials for about 500k companies, it gives outcome labels (default, restructuring and recovery results). Registr smluv holds millions of full-text public contracts. The data is available through web registries and some APIs. Bulk access is imperfect, and KRZ has no bulk download.
r2.current_users: KRUK (market cap about $2B), Best SA, PRA Group, Intrum and Hoist all price NPLs with large proprietary recovery datasets. BIK, Infomonitor, Creditinfo, Dun & Bradstreet/Bisnode, Rejestr.io and Hlídač státu (an NGO that mines the Czech Registr smluv) also use this data. The incumbents' private recovery data beats the public registers.
r2.ml_unlock: Learning from the creditor lists in every restructuring which suppliers are exposed to which failing companies and what they recovered, so trade claims in restructurings can be priced and supply-chain contagion predicted. This is an angle that KRUK-style consumer-debt buyers don't cover.
r2.path_to_1B: Weak. Polish restructuring claims trading is a niche (thousands of proceedings a year). The SME credit and NPL markets are large but owned by incumbents that have better labels. Reaching $1B would require taking it across the EU under the Restructuring Directive (2019/1023) registers, which are not uniform.
r2.why_now: KRZ has accumulated about 5 years of digitised proceedings, and the EU Insolvency Directive harmonisation is underway.
r2.verified: Searched and confirmed: KRZ exists, went live in December 2021, and discloses proceedings and debtors (Taylor Wessing, Bankier, poradnikprzedsiebiorcy). From memory: the Czech 340/2015 rule, the Slovak CRZ, and KRUK's scale.

r2.name: Estonian and Lithuanian per-company quarterly tax and monthly payroll nowcast for embedded B2B credit
r2.jurisdiction: Estonia and Lithuania (Latvia partially)
r2.legal_basis: Estonia's Tax and Customs Board (EMTA) has published every company's quarterly state taxes paid, labour taxes, taxable turnover and employee headcount since 2017, under the Taxation Act's disclosure provisions. Lithuania's Sodra publishes each employer's monthly headcount and average insured wage as open data. Estonia's e-Business Register holds all annual reports in machine-readable XBRL.
r2.dataset: Quarterly (EE) and monthly (LT) time series of turnover, payroll and headcount for every registered employer, effectively a near-real-time health signal for each company. Combined with XBRL annual reports and the court and insolvency registers, it provides default labels.
r2.current_users: Inforegister, Creditinfo, Rekvizitai.lt, Teatmik, the Lursoft/Bisnode group and Baltic fintech lenders (Bigbank, Inbank) already use it for scoring.

r2.verified: From memory only: the EMTA quarterly publication (high confidence) and the Sodra employer open data (medium-high confidence). Not searched.

r2.name: Australian NEM named next-day generator and battery bid stacks for an AI trader or merchant battery operator
r2.jurisdiction: Australia (National Electricity Market)
r2.legal_basis: Under the National Electricity Rules, AEMO publishes every scheduled participant's bids (price bands, availability and rebid reasons), named by unit (DUID), the next day on NEMweb. This is unusual: US ISOs mask bid identities for 3-6 months.
r2.dataset: Bid stacks and rebids at 5-minute granularity since 1998, named by participant and unit, together with dispatch, prices and FCAS. It is all free CSV through NEMweb and the MMSDM archive.
r2.current_users: The space is crowded. Tesla Autobidder, Fluence Mosaic, Habitat Energy, Edify, Enel X, Akaysha's in-house desk, Shell Energy and the gentailers' desks all mine it, along with academic and NEMOSIS tooling. It is also conceptually close to the rejected FERC EQR and ISO-queue ideas.
r2.ml_unlock: Learning each competitor's bidding policy (inverse reinforcement learning on named bid stacks) to forecast price spikes and strategic rebidding, then trading batteries and hedges against those forecasts.
r2.path_to_1B: Taking positions as a merchant battery operator or virtual trader is feasible, but the edge is already being competed away and the business needs heavy capital. A software-only play is crowded.
r2.why_now: A battery build-out of more than 10 GW is in progress and coal is retiring, so volatility is rising. Even so, many sophisticated players already exist.
r2.verified: From memory: AEMO publishes named bids next day (high confidence) and the list of competitors. Not searched.

r2.name: FDA rejection letters plus failed-trial results: a model that predicts approval odds and backs it with capital
r2.jurisdiction: US (FDA), plus EU CTIS as a second source
r2.legal_basis: FDAAA 801 / 42 CFR Part 11 requires sponsors to post summary results, including for failed and terminated trials, within 1 year of primary completion. Starting July 2025, FDA has been publishing Complete Response Letters (CRLs, its rejection letters, previously kept confidential): over 200 historical letters from 2020-24 for products later approved, then new CRLs shortly after issue, served through the openFDA 'transparency/completeresponseletters' API. Drug Trials Snapshots publish demographic and efficacy data for each approval. FDA advisory committee briefing documents and votes are also public.
r2.dataset: About 60k+ ClinicalTrials.gov records with posted results (structured endpoints, adverse events, enrollment, termination reasons), the CRL full texts, which spell out the deficiencies behind each rejection (CMC/manufacturing, efficacy, safety, trial design), FDA action dates (Drugs@FDA), adcomm transcripts and votes, and approval letters. Labels: approve, CRL, or trial-endpoint failure. Bulk download through the AACT database and the openFDA API.
r2.current_users: Intelligencia AI (ML probability-of-success forecasts, partnered with ZS and pharma), Citeline/Biomedtracker and Evaluate (analyst-built PoS estimates), IQVIA Asset Intelligence, specialist biotech hedge funds with in-house NLP, and IntuitionLabs, which has already written up the CRL dataset. The CRL corpus is new as of mid-2025 and no product is yet built mainly on it. Selling probability-of-success software is a crowded market. Taking capital risk on it is less so.
r2.ml_unlock: A model that reads the trial results, the protocol and the manufacturing and inspection history, and outputs a calibrated probability of approval and of a CRL, along with the likely CRL reason (for example CMC vs efficacy). Training on CRL text means it learns why the agency rejects, not just base rates. Use it to price risk: fund clinical-stage or pre-filing assets via synthetic royalties or R&D funding, write approval-contingent financing, or run an event-driven book on PDUFA dates.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers and counterparties: royalty and structured financing (Royalty Pharma, Blackstone Life Sciences, NovaQuest; well over $20B/yr deployed by my estimate, not verified), biotech M&A and licensing diligence, and event-driven funds. Software alone hits the same ceiling as Intelligencia, roughly tens of millions in ARR. The $1B path is a balance-sheet model: a life-sciences credit and royalty fund using its own regulatory-risk model, earning management fees plus carry and growing AUM into the billions. A further option is regulatory-risk insurance on PDUFA outcomes.
r2.why_now: The CRL disclosure policy dates from July/Sept 2025 and the corpus grows with every new rejection, so no incumbent has years of head start on it. LLMs can now turn unstructured CRLs, protocols and adcomm transcripts into features. Rates and a biotech funding gap are pushing companies toward non-dilutive royalty and structured financing.
r2.verified: Searched and verified: FDA's CRL publication and the openFDA CRL API (open.fda.gov, Hogan Lovells, KFF); Intelligencia AI exists and partners with ZS. From memory: FDAAA 801 rules, the AACT record counts, the size of royalty financing, Snapshots content.

r2.name: Industry safety studies published by EFSA (pesticides, feed, food additives): AI toxicology to replace guideline animal studies, and EU renewal-outcome forecasting
r2.jurisdiction: EU (EFSA, plus ECHA for REACH); US EPA OPP as a secondary source
r2.legal_basis: The Transparency Regulation (EU) 2019/1381 amended the General Food Law and has applied to applications since 27 March 2021. EFSA must proactively publish all studies, data and supporting information submitted by applicants for pesticide active substances, feed additives, GMOs, food enzymes and similar, after its confidentiality decisions, on OpenEFSA. Applicants must also notify EFSA in advance of every study they commission, so studies cannot be quietly dropped. Publication does not grant commercial reuse rights: data protection and copyright remain, and the Q&A says publication does not mean permission to use the data. In the US, FIFRA 10(g) gives access to study data only to people who affirm they are not acting for a multinational pesticide producer.
r2.dataset: Full GLP guideline study reports (OECD TG 4xx: repeat-dose tox, carcinogenicity, developmental and reproductive tox, ecotox on bees, fish and Daphnia, environmental fate) for every new or renewed active substance and feed additive since 2021, together with EFSA's peer-review conclusion (critical areas of concern, approve or non-renew). ECHA adds study summaries for about 25k REACH substances. The data are mostly PDFs and IUCLID dossiers on OpenEFSA and need heavy extraction.
r2.current_users: In-silico tox is crowded on public data: UL Solutions' RASAR read-across, built on REACH data; Insilica; Lhasa (Derek/Sarah); Instem/Leadscope; VeriSIM; and the agchem companies' own groups (Syngenta, Bayer). I found no company systematically mining OpenEFSA's full study reports and EFSA conclusions as labelled training data, unverified beyond one search.
r2.ml_unlock: Learn from thousands of complete regulatory studies, with dose-response data and the regulator's final verdict, to predict (a) guideline-study outcomes from structure plus cheap in-vitro data, cutting the roughly 10-12 year, ~$300M development path for a new crop-protection active (Phillips McDougall/AgbioInvestor figure, from memory), and (b) which existing actives EFSA will flag or non-renew (ED criteria, bee risk). That second prediction matters most to the companies deciding which products to defend or launch.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers: the about $5-6B/yr crop-protection R&D spend (from memory) and the regulatory-science CRO market. A software and NAMs tool alone tops out in the low hundreds of millions. The $1B paths: (1) an AI-native agchem or biologicals developer that uses the model to pick and de-risk its own actives and licenses them out, or (2) a generic or off-patent registration roll-up that buys or supports actives the model predicts will survive EU renewal and captures the market left when competitors exit. The same models carry over to food additives, cosmetics ingredients (EU animal-testing ban) and REACH.
r2.why_now: The 2021 regime has now been through about 4-5 years of dossiers, so a labelled corpus exists. LLM extraction makes the PDFs usable. The EU and EPA are moving away from animal testing (EPA NAMs roadmap, EU chemical-strategy roadmap), so regulators will accept validated in-silico evidence. The EU renewal cycle and political pressure on glyphosate and similar actives keep non-renewal risk high.
r2.verified: Searched: the Transparency Regulation applying from March 2021 with proactive publication (EFSA pages, Covington), and the Commission Q&A on reuse limits. From memory: what exactly OpenEFSA holds and its volume, the development cost and timeline figures, FIFRA 10(g), and the competitor list. The legal grey zone of training on published but protected studies is the main risk and needs counsel.

r2.name: Every new US alcohol label (TTB COLA) joined with control-state SKU sales: spotting breakout brands and buying stakes early
r2.jurisdiction: US (TTB federal; about 17 'control' states and jurisdictions that run the wholesale or retail liquor monopoly)
r2.legal_basis: The Federal Alcohol Administration Act requires a Certificate of Label Approval before any interstate alcohol SKU ships, and the COLA registry (label images, brand, bottler, class, approval date) is public and searchable. Because control states are public monopolies, they publish their own sales: the Iowa ABD publishes every wholesale liquor transaction, by store, SKU and date, from 2012 onward on data.iowa.gov, and PA, NH, OH, VA, NC, MI and others publish product sales or price lists.
r2.dataset: About 150k+ COLAs a year with label images and bottler identity (from memory). Iowa: tens of millions of transaction rows by store, item and date, with bottle price. Other control-state SKU sales and listing/delisting decisions. Labels: which new SKUs win distribution and grow sales across states.
r2.current_users: Iowa liquor sales is a well-worn Kaggle and teaching dataset. NielsenIQ, Circana, IWSR, BevAlc Insights and Park Street analytics sell trade data. Spirits majors' venture arms (Diageo Distill Ventures, Pernod) and some boutique brand investors scout brands. I know of no ML fund that combines COLA filings with control-state sales to underwrite investments.
r2.ml_unlock: An early-warning model: from a new COLA (category, label design, bottler or co-packer network, founder's past filings) plus the first months of control-state sell-through, predict which of thousands of new brands will break out nationally (Casamigos, High Noon type outcomes). Then invest before the majors do.
r2.path_to_1B: Buyers: spirits majors' M&A teams (Casamigos sold for up to $1B; frequent $100M-$1B brand exits, from memory) and brand-investor funds. A data subscription is a niche under $100M. The only $1B path is investing: a brand-holding company or fund that takes positions early, and the US category is softening (2024-26 volume decline), which weakens that case. The data is also only a proxy for sales outside control states.
r2.why_now: Vision-language models can read label images, and RTD and celebrity-brand launches multiplied. Alcohol category weakness makes cheap brand stakes available but lowers exit values.
r2.verified: Searched: the Iowa liquor sales open dataset (data.gov). From memory: the COLA registry's public status and volume, which control states publish sales, and deal sizes.

r2.name: Ship inspections and casualty records (Port State Control detentions, IMO GISIS) for marine insurance pricing
r2.jurisdiction: Global (Paris MoU THETIS, Tokyo MoU, USCG, IMO GISIS)

r2.name: FAA component failure reports (SDR) plus NASA ASRS for valuing used aircraft parts and engines
r2.jurisdiction: US (FAA), EU (EASA/ECCAIRS, which is less open)
r2.legal_basis: 14 CFR 121.703/125.409/135.415 require operators to report service difficulties (component failures and malfunctions). The FAA SDR database is public. NASA ASRS publishes de-identified voluntary safety reports. Airworthiness Directives are public.

shortlist.name: Contract-surety MGA priced on public DOT bid tabulations
merged_from: AI surety MGA for public-works contractors, priced on DOT bid tabulations plus bridge and pavement condition panels
Data-underwritten surety MGA for public-works contractors (bid-tab 'winner's curse' risk model)
shortlist.thesis: Public sealed-bid law (23 CFR 635 plus state bid-opening statutes) publishes every bidder's line-item prices on every DOT letting, and the Miller Act and state Little Miller Acts make every winner buy a bond. Model contractor default from four signals: winner's-curse spread (gap to the 2nd bid and to the engineer's estimate), unbalanced line-item bidding, backlog rebuilt from all wins across states, and change-order behaviour. Then write contract surety (and later subcontractor default insurance) as an MGA.
shortlist.why_selected: $1B path: US surety is about $8-9B DWP, of which contract surety is about $5B. An MGA writing $500M-1B of premium, or a carrier with a better loss ratio, is worth $1B+. The forced-disclosure edge is real. Incumbent sureties underwrite on CPA financials and agent relationships. No single surety sees a contractor's full cross-state backlog, but the bid tabs show it. InRev (workflow) and PinPoint/Edgevanta (estimating) are not doing risk pricing. Feasibility: download 5-10 years of bid tabs from one state DOT and compute spread and backlog features in a day. It was the top self-score in two separate lanes.
shortlist.key_unknowns: 1) Can default labels be got at scale? Miller Act suits in PACER, DOT default and termination notices, and surety claims are sparse and scattered. 2) Do change-order and final-cost records exist in bulk for enough states? 3) Does the winner's-curse spread actually predict surety loss beyond the financials? Check the academic literature and ask SFAA/Merchants. 4) Fronting capacity and appetite for a seed-stage surety MGA. 5) The surety loss ratio is 15-25% and losses are cyclical, so do reinsurers believe a model edge?

shortlist.name: SBA 7(a)/504 outcome-panel SMB credit engine (AI-native SBA lender or buyer of unguaranteed portions)
merged_from: SBA 7(a)/504 outcome-labelled SMB credit engine: an AI-native SBA lender, or a buyer of unguaranteed portions
shortlist.thesis: Under FOIA and its open-data policy, SBA publishes every 7(a) and 504 loan since about 1991 with borrower name and address, lender, NAICS, franchise code and outcome. Since March 2026 it also publishes live loan-level status (DELINQ, PURCH, LIQUID, CHGOFF). Join this to location and alternative data through the public address, train a market-wide PD/LGD model, and use it to originate SBA loans or price unguaranteed portions.
shortlist.why_selected: $1B path: Live Oak and Newtek show SBA-centric lenders reach $1-3B market caps. There are $8-12B a year of unguaranteed risk and a $1.4T SMB lending market. The quirk produces outcome labels at scale (about 2M+ loans over 30 years, and now monthly delinquency transitions), which no single lender has across the whole market. The 2026 disclosure change is a real why-now. Feasibility is the best on the list: one CSV download, and a cross-lender default model with franchise and ZIP effects can be built in a day. Existing vendors automate workflow, not outcome modelling.
shortlist.key_unknowns: 1) Will SBA keep refreshing the status fields, given policy volatility? 2) Recovery and LGD amounts are not cleanly disclosed. 3) How much lift there is over the FICO/SBSS/FRANdata baselines lenders already use. 4) Licensing route: SBLC licence, bank charter or partner bank, and capital needs. 5) Does Live Oak or a quant SMB lender already do this internally?

Train one model across all of them to estimate each carrier's true ultimate losses per line, and use it to price loss-portfolio transfers and adverse-development covers, and to back a run-off or sidecar vehicle.

The LPT/ADC market writes tens of billions a year, and US casualty is in a social-inflation reserve-strengthening cycle. Labels at scale are built into the filing structure. Feasibility: CAS publishes a free cleaned Schedule P dataset, so a cross-company deep-learning reserving model against chain-ladder can be backtested in a day.

shortlist.name: PAGA wage-and-hour liability MGA (CA LWDA notice plus settlement corpus)

deep.name: Contract-surety MGA priced on public DOT bid tabulations (adversarial review: weak, do not lead with it)
deep.legal_basis_verified: Partly verified. 23 CFR 635.112-114 requires competitive sealed bids, publicly opened, for federal-aid highway construction, and all 50 state DOTs publish bid tabs with every bidder's line-item prices. I confirmed this for TxDOT, which has a bid-tab dashboard and Socrata datasets of bid items from ESBD and its electronic bidding system. The Miller Act (40 USC 3131) applies to federal contracts over $150k, and state Little Miller Acts cover state and local public works (from memory, standard law). So the forced disclosure is real. But it only covers the public, horizontal, low-bid slice of contract surety. Private, vertical and subcontract bonds, and design-build and CMAR (best-value, not low-bid) work, produce no bid tabs. The supposed key signal, cross-state backlog, is not secret either. Every bonded contractor already gives its surety a work-in-progress schedule each quarter or year, listing all of its jobs, public and private. That is better backlog data than the bid tabs give.
deep.data_access: Bid tabs are on roughly 50 DOT portals, in PDF, Excel and HTML. Many are AASHTOWare Project exports, and many are behind Bid Express (Infotech), which is licensed and partly paywalled for bulk history. Texas has the cleanest feed. data.texas.gov / data.austintexas.gov Socrata dataset qh8x-rm8r ("Official and Unofficial Bid Items") exports CSV, JSON and XML at https://data.austintexas.gov/api/v3/views/qh8x-rm8r/export.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD. Dataset de7b-7dna ("Bid Tabulations") holds only a rolling 24 months. There are also third-party Apify TxDOT scrapers. Volume is about $100B a year of state DOT lettings, roughly 10-20k contracts and millions of bidder x item rows a year nationally. I found no mirror on BigQuery public datasets, the AWS Open Data Registry, Zenodo or PyPI. The proof container (github, pypi, s3, googleapis only) probably cannot reach data.texas.gov or the DOT sites, so the proof data has to be fetched elsewhere and pushed to GitHub or S3. Default labels are the real gap. Miller Act suits are in PACER (paid, sparse). DOT default and termination notices are scattered and often only available through FOIA. Surety claim data is private to carriers. There are perhaps a few hundred contractor failures a year nationally, which is too few labels for a confident model without a carrier data partner. Final-cost and change-order data varies by state and is often FOIA-only.
deep.competitors: The direct "AI surety" space is small but not empty, and the idea is old in academia. InRev: digital surety MGA, $3.8M from Accelerant and Scrappy, workflow automation. PledgX (Canada): AI contractor prequalification and surety marketplace, $570k pre-seed, a NASBP partner. Adel Awad's 2012 U Alberta PhD, "Intelligent Contractor Default Prediction Model for Surety Bonding", shows the concept was studied 14 years ago. Bid-spread and winner's-curse economics also exist in the literature: Calveras, Ganuza and Hauk (2004) "Wild bids" on surety and abnormally low bids, and the De Silva, Dunne and Kosmopoulou line of Oklahoma DOT and Texas bid-data papers (from memory). On the bid-data side, PinPoint Analytics ($3.2M, HG Ventures), Edgevanta, Infotech/Bid Express and Oman Systems serve estimators, and Dodge/ConstructConnect have award feeds that sureties already buy. The incumbent market per SFAA Q3 2025 YTD, about $8.86B DWP: Liberty Mutual 12.3%, Travelers 12.2%, CNA 6.5%, Zurich 5.9%, Chubb 5.2%, Intact 3.0%, Hartford 2.7%, Merchants 2.6%, Crum & Forster 2.2%, Berkshire 2.0%. The top 10 hold about 54%. Merchants and others already run fast-track, credit-scored programs for small contractors. Shepherd ($42M) does construction casualty, not surety. I found no one explicitly pricing surety from bid-spread features. The likely reason is that the feature is weak relative to WIP and financials, not that nobody thought of it.
deep.product_and_wedge: The wedge is a risk score and early-warning feed for existing sureties and surety agents (NASBP members). It would flag each bonded contractor's public wins across all states, the gap to the 2nd bid and the engineer's estimate on each job, unbalanced line items, sudden jumps in bidding aggressiveness, and DOT performance-evaluation hits. Sell it as SaaS to the top 100 sureties' claims and underwriting teams, which also builds the labeled-loss partnership needed. Later, launch an MGA for small and DBE contractors (bond lines under $5M) that incumbents serve poorly, on fronted capacity.
deep.path_to_1B: Market: SFAA puts total US surety DWP at $8.86B through Q3 2025, about $11-12B annualized. Contract surety is about 60%, so roughly $6.5-7B (the split is from memory). Public low-bid work with bid tabs is perhaps 30-40% of contract surety, so about $2-2.5B of premium is directly addressable by the data. Bond rates run about 0.5-1.5% of contract value, and $100B of DOT lettings gives only about $0.7-1B of highway premium. Path A, MGA: to reach a $1B valuation you need about $500M-1B of premium, which is 20-40% of the addressable bid-tab slice. That is implausible for a new entrant in a relationship- and agent-driven line where Liberty and Travelers alone hold 25%. Path B, SaaS to sureties: about 100 meaningful buyers at roughly $100-300k each is about $10-30M ARR, a niche similar to the rejected $100-200M class. Path C, adjacencies: subcontractor default insurance (Zurich SDI, roughly $1B+ of premium, concentrated among large GCs) and contractor working-capital lending against awarded contracts (Billd- and Built-type players already exist). A $1B outcome needs Path A at scale or a lending business, and neither is unlocked mainly by bid tabs.
deep.revolutionary_claim: The claim is that public sealed-bid disclosure lets you see every contractor's pricing behaviour and public backlog across all states, and spot the winner's-curse jobs that precede default, before the annual CPA statement does. Adversarial verdict: this is incremental. Surety loss ratios are already about 20% (20.7% in 2025, 26.4% in 2024). Most of the cost is commission and expense, and losses come from a handful of large-account defaults that are lumpy and cyclical, so a better loss model moves little enterprise value. Indemnity agreements and salvage further mute the payoff from selection.
deep.proof_idea: Pull TxDOT bid items through the Socrata CSV, plus archived letting PDFs, for about 10 years. Compute per-job money left on the table (low bid vs 2nd bid vs engineer's estimate), line-item unbalancing scores and rolling public backlog per contractor. Labels: TxDOT contractor default and termination actions or suspended-contractor lists, Miller Act and Texas Govt Code 2253 payment-bond suits from CourtListener/RECAP (a free PACER mirror, reachable through its API), and contractors who drop out of bidding. Show that the top decile of spread-and-backlog risk has a materially higher 24-month default or exit rate, and test whether the lift survives controls for size and prequalification capacity. Risk: the label count may be under 100, making the result statistically fragile. Container caveat: the data must be staged to GitHub or S3 first.
deep.killers: 1) The economics punish a pure data edge. The surety loss ratio is about 20%, and the cost stack is mostly 25-30% commission plus expense. A better default model saves a few points of an already small loss ratio, and losses are dominated by rare, large, cyclical defaults (2024's spike came from "a handful of large-account defaults"). Reinsurers will not credit a model without a decade of loss history. 2) The backlog edge is illusory. Sureties already get full WIP schedules (public and private jobs) and indemnity from owners, which is richer than public wins. 3) Labels are scarce. Contractor defaults are a few hundred a year nationally, scattered across PACER, state courts and DOT notices, and claim data sits with carriers. 4) Coverage is narrow. Bid tabs cover only low-bid public work, while design-build, CMAR, private, vertical and subcontract bonds (a large part of premium) have none. 5) Distribution and capacity lock-in. Contract surety is sold through about 1,000 specialist agents tied to Liberty, Travelers, CNA and Merchants. A seed MGA needs fronting plus reinsurance on a long-tail credit line, and surety treaty terms tightened after renewable-energy losses (Aon). Small contractors are where losses are worst, which is why incumbents avoid them. 6) The idea is old: an academic default model exists (Awad 2012) and so does winner's-curse auction literature, and InRev and PledgX occupy the surety-tech slot. 7) Market math: reaching $1B needs about 20-40% of the addressable bid-tab premium. 8) Bulk access is messy (50 portals, a partly paywalled Bid Express) and not mirrored on BigQuery or AWS.

deep.name: SBA 7(a)/504 outcome-panel SMB credit engine (AI-native SBA lender or buyer of unguaranteed portions). Verdict: crowded. Lumos Data already sells this, with Live Oak's CEO as an investor.
deep.legal_basis_verified: Mostly verified. SBA publishes the "7(a) & 504 FOIA" dataset on data.sba.gov under FOIA (5 USC 552) and its Open Government policy, so the files exist as a FOIA-driven release. Coleman Report confirms that from the 3/31/2026 data cut SBA discloses each 7(a) loan's current status: CURR, PIF, CANCLD, PURCH (NOT C/O), CHGOFF, LIQUID, COMMIT, DELINQ, PSTDUE, DEFERD, CLSLN and EXEMPT. The FY2020-present file is "asof 260331". It was last updated 2026-04-28 and is 143.8 MiB. Refreshes are roughly quarterly (asof 251231, then 260331), but SBA has made no formal commitment to a schedule. Statuses appear to be confirmed for 7(a) only. Two caveats. First, the data is a quarterly snapshot, not a history: you must archive every release yourself to build delinquency transitions. Second, recovery and LGD are only partly observable (gross charge-off amount yes, net recoveries no). The policy risk is real: the disclosure is an administrative choice, not a statutory mandate, so SBA can stop it.
deep.data_access: Primary source: https://data.sba.gov/en/dataset/7-a-504-foia. CSVs are split by vintage (FY1991-99, FY2000-09, FY2010-19, FY2020-present, and 504 files) plus a data dictionary ("7a_504_FOIA Data Dictionary as of 251231.xlsx"). The FY2020+ file alone is 143.8 MiB; the full set is about 1-2 GB of CSV, about 1.6-2M+ 7(a) loans plus about 300k 504 loans. Fields include borrower name and address, lender, NAICS, franchise code, gross amount, guaranteed amount, term, jobs, status, charge-off date and gross charge-off. Licence: US government work, public domain. Mirrors reachable from the proof container: (1) AWS Data Exchange, where Enigma has a free "SBA Loans 7A/504" product delivered as S3 CSV objects. It is stale (only to 2019) and needs an ADX subscription, so it is not anonymous S3. (2) GitHub: many repos hold the Kaggle "SBAnational.csv" (899k loans, FY1987-2014, with MIS_Status CHGOFF/PIF labels, from the Li, Mickel and Taylor 2018 teaching paper), e.g. mehdi-jafarov/SBA-Default-Risk-Prediction. (3) An Apify scraper actor exists. None of the mirrors carry the 2026 status fields. data.sba.gov itself is not on the reachable-host list, so a proof run would use the GitHub copies of SBAnational.csv for historical PD. The new status panel would need a manual download pushed to GitHub or GCS.
deep.competitors: 1) Lumos Data (Wilmington NC) is the direct killer. Its Prime+ score is "built exclusively on small business loan data" with "30 years of performance data" and predicts 12-month PD and lifetime expected loss. It claims up to 35% lift over bureau scores and has 80+ financial-institution clients. It raised a $2M seed (2024) with Live Oak CEO Chip Mahan participating. It uses SBA default rates by county and has partnerships with FRANdata, Vertical IQ, Lenders Cooperative and Baker Hill (LOS distribution). 2) FRANdata's FUND scores are franchise-brand risk scores explicitly correlated with SBA loan performance, which covers the franchise-survival wedge. 3) FICO SBSS is already required for SBA 7(a) small loans. 4) Workflow vendors such as Biz2X, Lendio, Multimodal, Baker Hill, Abrigo/Sageworks and Ventures. 5) Balance-sheet players already price this risk in house: Live Oak (about 2.5% of 7(a) volume and its own 15-year loss dataset), Newtek, Ready Capital, Huntington. Unguaranteed-portion buyers and securitizers are also active: Momentus Securities (single-lender unguaranteed securitization platform, Jan 2025), Guidehouse (multiparty unguaranteed securitizations), and buyers such as Ready Capital and Bayview. 6) Academic and Kaggle: SBA default prediction is a standard classroom dataset (JSE 2018, GWU theses, the CSUS 2024 analytics competition), so a "cross-lender PD model on SBA FOIA" is commoditised as a concept. 7) ai-analytics.org and searchfunder tools already publish SBA default dashboards. Gap that remains: no one appears to productise the new 2026 monthly delinquency-transition panel or to take principal risk with a public-data model. That gap is thin and can be copied within one quarter.
deep.product_and_wedge: Best-case wedge: a "servicing early-warning plus portfolio benchmarking" feed for the roughly 1,500 SBA lenders. It would archive every quarterly status snapshot, model CURR to DELINQ to PURCH transitions by lender, NAICS, franchise and ZIP, and show each lender its own book against the market's. The business would then evolve into a buyer of unguaranteed portions or SMB loan pools priced off the panel plus alternative data joined through borrower name and address (reviews, permits, foot traffic, PPP history). This collides directly with Lumos, which already sits inside the Baker Hill and Lenders Cooperative LOS channels with Live Oak's blessing. The principal-risk version (a fund or lender) is differentiated only if the alternative-data join produces large lift, and that is unproven.
deep.path_to_1B: There is a path, but it runs through being a lender, not through the data. 7(a) approvals were about $31B+ in FY2025 (record level, consistent with SBA reports), so unguaranteed exposure is about $8-12B a year. Live Oak (market cap about $1.5-2B) and Newtek (about $0.3-0.5B) show that SBA-centric balance sheets reach $1B+. Live Oak needed a bank charter, more than 15 years and vertical expertise rather than public-data ML. SaaS-only math fails: 1,500 SBA lenders at $30-100k ACV is $45-150M TAM, which repeats the $100-200M niche that was rejected. Lumos, with 80+ FIs, is evidence of that ceiling. A $1B outcome requires (a) buying or chartering a lender or SBLC, and the SBLC moratorium and 2025 SOP 50 10 8 tightening make new licences hard, or (b) raising a $100M+ credit fund for unguaranteed portions or SMB pools. Both are capital-intensive and slow, are not natural YC shapes, and the edge must survive the fact that incumbents hold richer private data (bank statements, payment history) than the public file.
deep.revolutionary_claim: Weak. The claim would be the first market-wide, monthly-updated SMB default-transition model built from mandated public disclosure, joined to location and alternative data through public borrower addresses. In practice, cross-lender SBA default modelling has existed for years: Lumos ("30 years of performance data"), FRANdata FUND and academic work. The only new element is the 2026 status snapshot, which is an incremental feature, not a new capability.
deep.proof_idea: 1) From GitHub, pull the SBAnational.csv mirror (899k loans, CHGOFF/PIF labels). Train gradient-boosted PD with leakage-safe features available at origination (NAICS, franchise, ZIP, lender, term, guarantee %, urban/rural, vintage macro). Report out-of-time AUC on 2008-2010 vintages against a NAICS+state baseline.
