deep.name: Schedule P cross-carrier reserve model for pricing run-off (LPT/ADC) deals and casualty reinsurance
deep.legal_basis_verified: Mostly sound, from knowledge plus CAS confirmation. Every state's insurance code requires domestic P&C insurers to file the NAIC Annual Statement Blank, which includes Schedule P, "Analysis of Losses and Loss Expenses": 10-year paid, incurred and bulk/IBNR triangles plus claim counts for about 20 lines. Statutory statements are public records. The catch is that they are public to look at, not free in bulk. You can view or order one company's PDF from a state DOI or NAIC, but machine-readable bulk data across all companies is sold by NAIC (Financial Data Repository / InsData), S&P Capital IQ Pro, AM Best and FactSet, which has a "Schedule P Reserves" product. CAS confirms it compiled Schedule P research data from NAIC Schedule P and has extended it with accident years 1998-2007; access is by request to CAS Research. So the law creates the disclosure, but commercial vendors control bulk access. Fit to the brief: this is a genuine law-forced disclosure of realized outcomes (what reserves actually became), but it is aggregated at company x line x accident year, not at claim level.
deep.data_access: 1) The free research set is the CAS Loss Reserving Database. It covers 6 lines (private passenger auto, commercial auto, workers' comp, medical malpractice, other liability, product liability) for accident years 1988-1997, with a 10x10 triangle per company plus the lower-triangle realizations, about 100-200 companies per line, as CSV. CAS has since added accident years 1998-2007, available on request (licence not stated publicly). This set is mirrored on GitHub and PyPI-reachable routes: the R package 'raw' on CRAN/r-universe (casact.r-universe.dev, NAIC dataset), Ractuary/casdata on GitHub, Kevin Kuo's DeepTriangle/insurance repos on GitHub, and ChainLadder test data. All are reachable from github.com, so a backtest can run inside the proof container today. 2) The full universe (about 2,500 companies x 20 lines x 30+ filing years, plus Schedule F and the state Exhibit) is NOT free and NOT on AWS Open Data or BigQuery. It is licensed from NAIC, S&P Capital IQ Pro, AM Best or FactSet. Expect five to low-six figures a year, and redistribution terms restrict reselling derived data. 3) The deal-relevant data (claim-level loss runs and case files from the cedent) is private and only appears in a deal data room.
deep.competitors: Heavily served. Every reserving actuary already uses this data; it is not a hidden dataset. (a) WTW ResQ Machine-led Reserving, launched October 2024: automated ML-optimized reserving that WTW says shows "significant outperformance" over human picks in backtests, sold into the dominant reserving software. (b) LCP InsurSight: free and paid benchmarking of US P&C reserves from statutory filings. (c) FactSet, S&P and AM Best package Schedule P reserve-adequacy analytics, and AM Best's BCAR and S&P's capital model already run reserve-adequacy estimates on every carrier. (d) Milliman, Aon, Gallagher Re, Guy Carpenter, Swiss Re and Munich Re publish annual industry reserve-deficiency studies by line from Schedule P, the source of the social-inflation reserve estimates. (e) Sell-side (KBW, Dowling, Morgan Stanley) and insurance hedge funds already screen Schedule P for reserve deficiency; it is the standard short thesis. (f) Academics: DeepTriangle (Kuo 2019), stacked ANN (arXiv 2008.07564), and a 2026 R package, mlreserve, for ML reserving on real-world triangles. (g) Run-off and legacy capital: Enstar (Sixth Street take-private), Fortitude Re, Catalina, Compre, Premia, Riverstone, Carrick Re, Maiden's Genesis Legacy Solutions, and RiverStone/Arch-type players, each with in-house actuarial teams and Big-4 due diligence. I found no venture startup whose core product is a cross-carrier ML Schedule P model, but that is because the incumbents (WTW, the rating agencies, data vendors and reinsurer research teams) already occupy that ground, not because the space is empty.
deep.product_and_wedge: Wedge: a "true ultimate" API giving per-carrier, per-line ultimate losses and reserve-deficiency estimates with uncertainty, trained jointly across all carriers, with a calibrated backtest against chain-ladder/BF on CAS data and NAIC data from 1988 to 2015. First buyers would be insurance equity and credit hedge funds (short under-reserved carriers), legacy acquirers and ADC reinsurers screening targets, and M&A advisors. Next step is an MGA with fronted capacity or a sidecar that offers ADCs and LPTs on carriers the model rates as over-reserved, priced tighter than incumbents. Honest limit: a public-data model is a screening and prior tool. Binding prices are set on cedent claim-level data with claims-handling diligence, so the edge works only at the top of the funnel (picking targets) or in trading the equity and credit, not as the underwriting engine itself.
deep.path_to_1B: The bottom-up math is weak. Mayer Brown, citing PwC, reports only about $1.1B of gross reserves in publicly announced non-life run-off deals from January to August 2025 (25 deals), versus $6.6B in 2024. Including private and Lloyd's RITC/ADC deals, global legacy flow is plausibly $10-30B of reserves a year (from memory), not "tens of billions written" with fat margins. Legacy margins are thin: roughly 3-8% of reserves over the life of the deal, earned through claims management and investment float. To reach $1B you would need a balance-sheet run-off consolidator holding about $10-20B of reserves (Enstar-scale; Sixth Street's 2025 take-private of Enstar at about $5.1B is from memory, not verified here). That requires billions of equity, a claims-handling operation and regulatory licences: years of capital raising, not a YC software path. Software alone: reserving and analytics software TAM is about $100-300M and dominated by WTW ResQ, Arius (Milliman), Moody's and Aon. A hedge-fund route (trading insurer equities on reserve signals) could scale on AUM but is not a venture-backable startup. Bottom line: a credible $1B path exists only as a capital-heavy legacy carrier where ML is a minor edge. It fails the user's $1B filter in practice.
deep.revolutionary_claim: Weak. Cross-company learning from triangles is the point of Schedule P, and actuaries have done it for decades: industry development factors, Bornhuetter-Ferguson priors from industry loss ratios, and the CAS benchmark studies. The literature finds deep-learning reserving (DeepTriangle and successors) beats chain-ladder by single-digit to roughly 20% RMSE on the CAS data, with gains concentrated in volatile small-company triangles. That is an incremental improvement, not a step change. The "revolutionary" version would be predicting carrier-level reserve charges 2-3 years early from cross-carrier signals plus filing text, which sell-side analysts and AM Best already attempt manually.
deep.proof_idea: In one day: pull the CAS Schedule P CSVs via the GitHub/CRAN mirrors (casact 'raw' package, Ractuary/casdata). For each of the 6 lines, train a pooled cross-company model (gradient boosting or a GRU in the DeepTriangle style, with company embeddings) on the upper triangles and predict the lower-triangle ultimate. Compare RMSE/MAPE on ultimate losses and reserve adequacy against per-company chain-ladder, Mack and BF with industry ELR. Also test whether the model ranks the companies that later took the largest adverse development (top decile) better than chain-ladder does: that ranking is the tradable signal. Kill criterion: under 15% error reduction, or no lift in top-decile adverse-development detection over a BF industry prior.
deep.killers: 1) Not hidden data. Schedule P is the most-analyzed public dataset in P&C insurance; every rating agency, reinsurer, broker, consultant and insurance hedge fund already mines it, and WTW shipped ML-led reserving in 2024. The "nobody sees cross-company patterns" premise is false: industry triangles are standard practice. 2) The labels are aggregated, lagged and managed. Carriers smooth reserves, and commutations, reinsurance (net vs gross), M&A pooling, and changes in line definitions and reporting add noise. 10-year triangles mean ultimate labels for casualty arrive 10-20 years late. 3) The free data stops at accident year 2007 and is small (a few hundred companies x 6 lines). The full dataset is licensed, and vendor terms limit derivative resale. 4) Legacy and ADC deals are priced on claim-level cedent data plus claims-operations diligence, so a public aggregate model adds little at the binding-price stage. 5) Legacy deal flow is lumpy and recently down (about $1.1B of public reserves January-August 2025, versus $6.6B in 2024), margins are thin, and R&Q's 2024 failure shows the risk of mispricing. 6) A risk vehicle needs a rated balance sheet, regulators and billions of capital, which is a bad fit for a first-time founder at YC. 7) Distance from the founder's edge: it needs credentialed actuaries (FCAS) to be credible with counterparties. 8) Gains are academically modest (DeepTriangle-scale), so incumbents can copy them easily.

deep.name: PAGA wage-and-hour liability MGA (CA LWDA notice and settlement corpus). Verdict: weak. The data edge is real but the insurance wedge is mostly blocked by law and adverse selection.
deep.legal_basis_verified: Verified. Cal. Labor Code 2699.3 requires a PAGA claim notice to be filed with the LWDA ($75 fee) before suit. Section 2699(s), renumbered after the 2024 reform, requires proposed settlements to be submitted to the LWDA when they go to court, and orders or judgments within 10 days of entry. DIR's PAGA page says notices are "public records and subject to disclosure to any member of the public" (fee-waiver requests are confidential) and that older records "may be destroyed under agency policy". So history may be incomplete. There is an online case and document search (cadir.my.salesforce-sites.com/PagaSearch). The page mentions no bulk download or export. Public Records Act requests go to PAGAinfo@dir.ca.gov. Volume, verified via Ankura's 2026 update: 9,437 notices in the 12 months before the June 2024 reform, 8,971 in the year to June 2025, 8,762 in the year to June 2026, and 8,846 in LWDA fiscal year 2024-25 (about 34 per workday). The reform cut penalties, added cure and penalty caps, and shifted notice volume by industry: logistics down 27%, janitorial down 29%, senior living up 10%, healthcare up 8%. Filing is very concentrated: 20 of 396 plaintiff firms filed 50% of notices. Unfavourable law, from memory and supported by the coverage literature I found (Wiley alert on Classic Distributing v. Travelers, SHRM's "EPLI often excludes wage-hour"): unpaid wages are restitution, so not insurable "loss". Cal. Ins. Code 533 and public policy bar coverage of wilful acts, and many policies and courts treat penalties as uninsurable or exclude them. In practice the insurable part is mainly defense costs, plus arguably PAGA civil penalties. Not verified: whether carriers would cover PAGA penalties post-reform.
deep.data_access: Primary source: the LWDA PAGA search, a Salesforce Sites app at https://cadir.my.salesforce-sites.com/PagaSearch. Records are searchable per case with PDF attachments (notice letter, employer response or cure, proposed settlement, order). There is no bulk API or download, so you would have to scrape it or ask for bulk exports by PRA request. About 9k notices a year since the 2016 online portal, roughly 80-90k notices in total. Settlement PDFs cover a fraction of cases: many notices never reach a filed settlement, and many settle inside class actions that only describe the PAGA allocation. Fields need OCR and LLM extraction: gross settlement, PAGA allocation (65/35 split after reform), class size, fees, employer name. Entity resolution from employer name to a firm is hard (DBAs, staffing agencies, joint employers). Mirrors: none found. I found no GitHub repos, PyPI packages, AWS Open Data, BigQuery or Zenodo copies; only adjacent CA WARN scrapers on Apify and warn-scraper. So the proof container (github/pypi/s3/googleapis only) cannot reach the LWDA data. A proof needs data pulled elsewhere and pushed to a GitHub repo or GCS bucket. Ankura has a proprietary PAGA settlement database already built from these filings, which shows the corpus can be built and also that someone already holds it. Joinable public features: DOL WHD compliance-action CSVs (enforcedata.dol.gov, nationwide back wages by employer), CA WARN, pay-range postings, and court dockets via Trellis or Docket Alarm.
deep.competitors: Data and analytics: Ankura publishes PAGA trend reports from a proprietary LWDA notice and settlement database with industry classification. CABIA (business lobby) and defense-firm coalitions analyse the same corpus for policy. Lex Machina, Trellis, Docket Alarm and UniCourt cover state-court wage-hour dockets. Plaintiff firms mine notices informally; 20 firms make half the filings. Compliance software: Scaled Comp (2025, AI time-record structuring for CA wage-hour defense; funding not stated). Payroll and HR platforms (Rippling, Gusto, Justworks, ADP, Paycom) and timekeeping tools that flag meal and rest violations; Legion and Deputy do scheduling compliance. Insurance: standalone wage-and-hour products have been tried and stayed niche, e.g. Aon Risk Solutions' wage-hour facility (2012) and XL Group's Wage & Hour Liability coverage (2013), plus a few Lloyd's and E&S markets. Those are defense-plus-settlement towers for large employers with retentions often $1M+ and thin take-up. Mainstream EPLI (Chubb, AIG, Beazley, Travelers, USLI) gives defense-only sublimits, typically $100-250k (USLI enhanced its EPL form in Nov 2025). PEOs (Insperity, TriNet, Justworks) carry co-employment exposure and buy master EPLI. No funded startup found that underwrites wage-hour risk from LWDA data. That gap looks like an insurability gap, not a data gap.
deep.product_and_wedge: Best wedge, reframed away from the MGA: a PAGA exposure score and notice-probability model sold to (a) PEOs and EPLI carriers for pricing defense-cost sublimits and choosing which CA risks to write, (b) R&W/M&A insurers and buyers, since RWI policies routinely exclude CA wage-hour and a model-priced, deal-specific buyback is a new product, and (c) employers' general counsel as a benchmark ("your peer group's 12-month notice probability and expected settlement per employee"). Only later, write a defense-plus-PAGA-penalty product via an MGA for employers whose payroll and timekeeping data feed the model directly. That continuous-monitoring feed is the only real answer to moral hazard. The pure MGA for wage indemnity in the original thesis is not viable as a wedge.
deep.path_to_1B: Weak. Loss pool: about 8.8k notices a year. If about 50-60% resolve with a payment at an average gross of roughly $0.5-1.5M (Ankura's sample: values flat after reform; amounts from memory, not verified), CA wage-hour and PAGA resolutions are about $2-5B a year. But most of that is wages owed (restitution, uninsurable) plus plaintiff fees. The insurable slice is defense costs (about $150-500k per matter) plus arguably PAGA penalties. That is perhaps $1-2B a year of insurable loss, implying about $1.5-3B of potential premium at 60-70% loss ratios, assuming very high take-up among the roughly 1M+ CA employers with employees. Realistic MGA capture over 7-8 years: about $150-300M GWP at 15-20% commission is $25-60M revenue, not a $1B company on its own. Software and data sales to PEOs, carriers and RWI underwriters total maybe tens of carriers and about 500 PEOs, so a $50-150M revenue ceiling. Going multistate (NY, NJ, IL, WA) needs equivalent forced filings, which mostly do not exist. NY and NJ have no PAGA-style public notice corpus, and federal FLSA collectives are only in PACER. That caps the data moat at CA. A $1B outcome requires becoming the dominant employment-practices MGA nationally on general EPLI plus a CA wage-hour edge. That is a much bigger, more crowded insurtech bet in which this dataset is a feature. Overall this looks like the same $100-300M niche ceiling that was rejected before.
deep.revolutionary_claim: First actuarial base for California wage-and-hour liability: notice-to-settlement outcome labels for roughly 80k claims, which would turn a risk carriers exclude into a priced one. Adversarial view: carriers exclude it mainly because wages are uninsurable and violations are under the insured's control, not because data is missing. So the model's value is better pricing of a narrow defense-cost and penalty layer, which is incremental rather than revolutionary.
deep.proof_idea: Pull 1-2k PAGA cases (2019-2023 notices) from the PagaSearch portal off the proof container and push a parquet file to a GitHub repo. LLM-extract the employer, violation types, plaintiff firm and filing date from notices, and gross amount, PAGA allocation, class size and fees from linked settlement PDFs. Measure the link rate (share of notices with a settlement filed within 36 months) and extraction accuracy on 100 hand-checked cases. Then fit a notice-level model (industry, plaintiff firm, violation set, employer size from WARN or WHD joins) predicting settle/no-settle and log amount. Report AUC and calibration. Separately, backtest 12-month notice prediction for employers with prior WHD actions or notices. The kill condition: if the link rate is under 40% or amount R2 is under 0.3, the actuarial thesis is dead.
deep.killers: 1) Insurability: unpaid wages are restitution, Cal. Ins. Code 533 bars wilful acts, and penalty coverage is contested. The coverable layer is defense costs and maybe PAGA penalties, which shrinks the market by about 70%+. 2) Moral hazard and adverse selection: wage-hour violations are a choice by the insured, buyers self-select, and that is why the XL (2013) and Aon (2012) standalone products stayed tiny. 3) Ankura already holds a proprietary LWDA settlement database, and defense firms and CABIA analyse it, so the data edge is not unique. 4) There is no bulk access and no mirror. The Salesforce scrape is fragile, settlement linkage is incomplete (many PAGA claims settle inside class actions), and DIR may destroy older records. 5) CA-only: no equivalent forced public filing in other states, so the moat does not travel. 6) The 2024 reform cut penalties and allows cure, so post-reform loss is shrinking and old labels are biased for pricing. 7) There is legislative risk: further PAGA reform or LWDA's 2026 rulemaking could change the settlement-submission regime. 8) Selling PAGA risk scores also helps plaintiff firms target employers, a reputational and channel conflict with PEOs and employers. 9) A YC timeline cannot reach carrier or reinsurer capacity plus a CA DOI-licensed MGA by Nov 2026 with traction.

deep.name: DataJud-priced Brazilian legal-claims balance sheet (subnational precatórios, then litigation loss-portfolio transfers). Verdict: weak, do not pursue as the main idea.
deep.legal_basis_verified:
PARTLY VERIFIED, AND THE REGIME HAS CHANGED AGAINST THE THESIS.
(1) Constitution Art. 100 sets chronological payment, and CNJ Res. 303/2019 makes courts publish precatório lists. Courts do publish them (e.g. the TJCE 2026 minutes), but as PDF/HTML that differs court by court.
(2) CNJ Res. 331/2020 created DataJud, and its public API exists (CNJ page, pydatajud on PyPI, Apify actors). CRITICAL: the public API EXCLUDES party data (names, CPF and CNPJ, citing LGPD). It returns only class, subjects, court body, filing date, confidentiality level and coded movements. As far as can be found there is no valor da causa and no decision text. A single query returns at most 10,000 hits, so bulk pulls need search_after paging per court.
(3) EC 136/2025, promulgated 9 Sep 2025 from PEC 66/23 (verified via Câmara):
- State and municipal precatório payments are now capped at 1% of net current revenue (RCL) when the overdue stock is at or below 15% of RCL, rising to at most 5% when it exceeds 85% of RCL.
- Correction is cut to IPCA (plus 2%/yr interest, with Selic as a ceiling if that sum exceeds Selic) from Aug 2025.
- Federal precatórios leave the spending cap from 2026, with a stock of about R$70B.
This is the "regime risk" from the key unknowns, and it has already happened. Subnational paper now has much longer duration and lower yield.
(4) CPC Art. 835 §2 and CLT Art. 899 §11 do allow seguro garantia judicial instead of cash deposits. This is from memory and consistent with the press.
deep.data_access:
- **Endpoint:** DataJud public API at https://api-publica.datajud.cnj.jus.br/api_publica_{tribunal}/_search. Elasticsearch JSON, public API key published by CNJ, one index per court (27 TJs, TRF1-6, TRT1-24, TST, STJ, ...).
- **Content:** metadata and TPU-coded movements only. No parties or CNPJ, no case value, no texts. Results cap at 10k per query, so paging is required.
- **Volume:** tens of millions of cases. No bulk dump is published.
- **Precatório lists:** court-by-court PDFs and portals under Res. 303. Fiscal data (RCL) comes from Tesouro SICONFI's API (apidatalake.tesouro.gov.br).
- **Mirrors:** no DataJud mirror found on GitHub, PyPI (client only), AWS Open Data, BigQuery public datasets or Zenodo. Only small samples exist: the 4TU "Brazilian Justice Proceedings Dataset" (academic process-mining sample on data.4tu.nl), Apify scraper actors and GitHub wrapper repos such as joaotextor/busca-processos-judiciais.
- **Proof container:** it cannot reach cnj.jus.br, tesouro.gov.br or the court portals, so a proof must run off-container or from a pre-pulled extract uploaded to S3/GCS.
- **Licence:** public data under LAI/CNJ terms. LGPD restricts re-identifying parties.
deep.competitors:
CROWDED ON THE PRECATÓRIO SIDE.
- **Buyers and platforms:** Precato, Ativos Precatórios (Recife), Adianta Jus (now buying Correios precatórios), Hurst Capital and fintech structured-credit offers (Finsiders reports small raises such as R$1.6M), plus many brokers and law-firm cessionários.
- **Ativos' AI tool:** "Ativos Intelligence" (Apr 2026) is a broker assistant (negotiation arguments, value estimates). Per the fetched article it is NOT a risk-pricing model. It cost about R$300k to build and its platform has about 1,000 intermediaries.
- **Funds and banks:** BTG, XP, Itaú, Jive/Mauá, Valora, Kinea-type credit funds, and dozens of precatório FIDCs administered by Vórtx, BRL Trust and others.
- **Legal-data vendors** (no positions taken): Jusbrasil, Escavador, Digesto, Predictus, JUIT, Turivius, Deep Legal, Jurídico.ai, Cria.AI. These scrape court portals and get party names, which DataJud lacks.
- **Judicial surety:** Junto Seguros (R$1B+ in direct surety premium), Pottencial (2025 surety leader), Tokio Marine, Berkley, Swiss Re Corporate Solutions, Sompo, Fairfax.
- **Labor-litigation loss-portfolio transfer:** none found. Searches return only analytics and advisory firms. The likely reason is structural (see killers), not oversight.
- Searches found no YC company in this space.
deep.product_and_wedge:
- **Wedge:** a pricing engine for state and municipal precatórios (and pre-precatório claims at final-judgment stage).
- **Pricing inputs:**
  - queue position from the court's Res. 303 list
  - the debtor's RCL and overdue stock from SICONFI, giving its EC 136 payment cap of 1-5% of RCL
  - historical cap compliance and seizure (sequestro) behaviour
  - DataJud movement histories, for the odds of surviving recalculation or rescission and for the time from expedição to payment
- **Delivery:** an origination app for lawyers and brokers that gives instant firm bids, with purchases funded through a FIDC.
- **Expansion:** pricing judicial-guarantee bonds and contingency books for sureties, as an MGA.
- **Assessment:** after EC 136 the timing leg is largely a deterministic formula (cap × RCL ÷ queue ahead). That shrinks what ML adds.
deep.path_to_1B:
- **Stock:** reported at about R$330B in precatórios (press, not primary). Federal is about R$70B and already efficiently priced. The subnational long tail is the target.
- **Asset-manager math:**
  - Raising R$10B AUM in precatório FIDCs at 1.5-2% management fee plus 20% performance fee gives R$150-200M in management fees (about $30-40M) plus carry. At 15-20x fee-related earnings that is roughly $0.6-1B.
  - Retaining first-loss equity of R$1-2B at a 25% IRR adds R$250-500M a year.
- **Feasibility of the path:** reaching R$10B would make it one of the largest precatório managers in Brazil. Under EC 136, municipal paper now pays out at 1-5% of RCL a year, so turnover is slow and capital is locked up for longer, and IRR depends on discounts deep enough to offset IPCA+2% accrual.
- **Surety leg:** total Brazilian surety premium is about R$3-5B a year, and the judicial share is a subset. A 10% share is R$300-500M in premium, which supports an MGA worth hundreds of millions, not billions.
- **Overall:** a $1B outcome is possible but would require becoming the dominant capital provider in a market that is regulation-shocked and relationship-driven.
- **Sources:** Câmara (EC 136), Folha Vitória/Assertif (2022 surety R$3.4B premiums, 28% loss ratio), Revista Apólice (Pottencial 2025 leader), Monitor Mercantil (Junto R$1B).
deep.revolutionary_claim:
The first national, model-priced bid for any Brazilian court-ordered government debt, built on DataJud movement histories and fiscal capacity. Honest assessment: this is incremental, not revolutionary.
- After EC 136, payment timing is mostly a published fiscal formula.
- Survival of the claim (rescission, recalculation) is a small-variance term for claims that are already res judicata.
- Origination, not pricing, is what limits buyers.
deep.proof_idea:
Run off-container, because cnj.jus.br is not reachable from the proof box. Alternatively, pre-pull data to S3.
1. With pydatajud, pull every case of TPU class 1265 (Precatório) and the RPV classes from 2-3 TJs (TJSP, TJPE, TJBA) with full movements. Page with search_after.
2. Parse each TJ's Res. 303 chronological list to link the precatório number to the debtor entity.
3. Join the debtor's RCL and stock from the SICONFI API.
4. Label the time from expedição to the payment movement (TPU payment and levantamento codes), with survival censoring.
5. Fit a gradient-boosted survival model and compare it against a naive EC 136 formula baseline (cap% × RCL ÷ queue ahead).

Kill criterion: if the model doesn't beat the formula's C-index or calibration by a material margin on post-2025 data, there is no ML edge.

A side test: measure what share of pre-precatório claims gets recalculated downward. DataJud should show this through movement codes for impugnação/embargos à execução against the Fazenda.
deep.killers:
1. **Regime risk has already happened.** EC 136/2025 caps state and municipal payments at 1-5% of RCL, extending duration to decades for heavily indebted municipalities, and cuts correction to IPCA plus 2%. Repeated amendments (EC 62, 94, 99, 109, 113/114, 136) mean the core risk is political and cannot be learned from the data. Demarest reports the PEC froze the market and cut prices.
2. **Timing is now formula-driven.** It follows from published RCL, the overdue stock and the queue, so incumbents can compute it in a spreadsheet and the ML edge is thin.
3. **DataJud is thinner than the thesis assumes.**
   - No parties or CNPJ (LGPD), so it cannot link claims to debtors or rebuild corporate litigation books. That kills the "reconstruct every company's book by CNPJ" premise of leg 2.
   - No case values or texts, and a 10k cap per query.
   - The enrichment that matters (party names, amounts, calculation reports) needs scraping of court portals, which is the existing moat of Jusbrasil, Escavador and Digesto.
4. **The bottleneck is origination, not pricing.** Creditors are reached through lawyers and brokers, which is what Ativos' 1,000-intermediary network is. Assigning a precatório also requires court registration and has notary and tax frictions.
5. **Capital-heavy and local.** A FIDC needs a CVM administrator, a custodian and a local manager licence, and the business is fundraising-gated. A foreign founder has no network for origination, and it is a poor fit for YC's software profile.
6. **Leg 2 is structurally blocked.**
   - Brazilian labor liabilities cannot be legally transferred away from the employer, so any transfer is only an indemnity or reinsurance.
   - It needs a SUSEP licence and capital.
   - Judicial surety already runs a roughly 28% loss ratio on credit-based underwriting, so case-level models add little.
   - Courts (TST and TRTs) periodically reject or haircut insurance in place of deposits, and labor reform keeps shifting.
7. **FX and country risk** for USD-denominated investors.

deep.name: India IBC/SARFAESI recovery-pricing engine for a tech-enabled ARC/AIF (verdict: weak; reject as a YC candidate)
deep.legal_basis_verified:
Mostly real, but the claim of "every CIRP's claims, dual valuations and realisation" is overstated.
(1) IBC 2016 plus IBBI regulations. IBBI publishes NCLT orders (its repository listed about 29,466 NCLT records as of Mar 2025, per a DAKSH study) and quarterly newsletters. The newsletters tabulate resolved CIRPs: admitted FC claims, liquidation value, fair value where available, realisable amount and timeline. Liquidation outcomes are much thinner. The cumulative recovery rate was 32.1% of admitted FC claims as of Dec 2024 (DAKSH, citing IBBI).
(2) SARFAESI Act 2002 and the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules 2002, rules 8-9. Banks must publish the sale notice with reserve price in two newspapers, and PSBs list the property on the e-auction portal. BAANKNET has been operational since 1 Jul 2024 and was formally launched Jan 2025; it replaced e-Bikray (Feb 2019). Sale results are NOT systematically published. Only re-listings at a lower reserve act as implicit labels.
(3) Companies Act 2013 / MCA21: financials and charges are public, sold for a fee per document. Bulk access comes through resellers.
(4) eCourts/NJDG/DRT: open-court status and orders exist, but behind captchas, with no bulk API and grey legality for scraping.
DAKSH, the leading empirical group on this data, says NCLT orders are scanned images that are "not text searchable or machine readable". Order URLs change frequently, excluded periods and interim orders aren't reported, and category definitions shift over time, which breaks year-on-year comparison. The legal basis exists. The label quality is poor.

deep.name: FOAK technology-performance underwriter trained on forced public R&D final reports (OSTI/ARPA-E/SBIR/CORDIS/GtR)
deep.legal_basis_verified:
Partly verified, with a serious catch. EERE's Final Technical Report FAQ (EERE R 413.313) confirms the following. Every EERE financial-assistance award must deliver a Final Technical Report (FTR) through OSTI E-Link. FTRs without protected data are released on OSTI.GOV immediately. If the award authorises protected data, release can be held for up to 5 years after the period of performance. The FTR must contain "a comparison of the actual accomplishments with the goals and objectives of the project" and must describe problems and their impact. This is the target-versus-achieved field the thesis relies on.

The same rule says the FTR "must not contain ... proprietary, confidential, or business-sensitive information". Limited Rights data must be left out. DOE may also demand a scrubbed public version that is released immediately. The law therefore forces disclosure of whether goals were met, but lets the awardee withhold the quantitative performance numbers an underwriter wants most: yield, efficiency, cost per unit at scale.

SBIR data rights (20-year protection under the 2019 SBA policy directive, previously 4 years) cover much SBIR technical data. Phase I/II final reports are often thin or protected. Award metadata on SBIR.gov is public.

Not re-verified this round: Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement deliverable dissemination. Public deliverables are published on CORDIS, but most technical deliverables are marked "SEN" (sensitive) and are not public. UKRI GtR outcomes come from Researchfish and are mostly publication and IP counts, not performance data.

Net assessment: the forcing law is real, but it explicitly lets companies strip the commercially sensitive numbers. That differs from SMAD, where the raw assays themselves are what has to be filed.
deep.data_access:
**OSTI.GOV:** About 3M+ bibliographic records.
- Access: public REST API (osti.gov/api/v1/records) and OAI-PMH (listed on catalog.data.gov as "OAI-PMH for DOE Research and Development Reports").
- Format: metadata in JSON/XML, full text as PDF links. Rough guess: tens of thousands of financial-assistance FTRs from industry awardees.
- Licence: US government works, effectively public domain, though contractor-authored reports may carry notices.
- Mirrors: no known bulk mirror on GitHub, PyPI, AWS Open Data or BigQuery. OpenAlex indexes OSTI items and its snapshot is on S3 (s3://openalex, reachable), but that is metadata and abstracts only, not FTR full text. The PDFs would have to be pulled from osti.gov, which the proof container cannot reach.

**ARPA-E:** Project pages plus impact reports (HTML/PDF). No bulk export, scrape only. About 1,500+ projects.

**SBIR.gov:** Awards database with CSV/JSON downloads and an API, about 200k awards with Phase I/II linkage. Not mirrored on S3/BigQuery as far as I know. USAspending bulk files sit on files.usaspending.gov (S3-backed but a different host).

**CORDIS:** Project, organisation and deliverable metadata as CSV/JSON/XML via data.europa.eu (CC-BY 4.0). Public deliverable PDFs are linked. Not on S3/GCS.

**UKRI GtR:** REST API (gtr.ukri.org/api), Open Government Licence. Not mirrored.

**Outcome labels:**
- LPO portfolio: public HTML.
- EIA-860/923 plant generation: public; the PUDL project mirrors it on S3 and Zenodo (s3://pudl.catalyst.coop, reachable), which gives actual output against nameplate for power-generating FOAKs only.
- SEC EDGAR: reachable via the API, not S3.
- Bankruptcies: PACER.

Reachability from the proof container: realistically, only OpenAlex (S3) and PUDL/EIA (S3) can be reached directly. The core FTR full-text corpus would need a GitHub-hosted mirror built by us.

**Incumbent capacity providers (all price deal by deal, by hand, with in-house engineers):**

The uncrowdedness is probably because the data is weak, not because nobody has thought of it. New Energy Risk and Munich Re already have proprietary diligence data (full data rooms and independent-engineer reports) that is much richer than sanitised FTRs.
deep.path_to_1B:
**Top-down sizing:** RFF cites Javanmardian et al. (2022): about $800B of 2030 climate-tech capex implies $10-15B a year of associated insurance premium across all lines. Technology performance cover is a small slice of that.

**Bottom-up, today:**
- New Energy Risk has publicised about $500M+ of insured project value at milestones, which implies tens of policies a year.
- At 2-5% rate on line, global technology performance insurance GWP today is probably $50-300M a year. This is my estimate, not sourced.

**Bull case (2030-32):**
- 40 FOAK/NOAK projects a year wrapped, averaging $500M covered value, gives $20B covered. At 2% that is $400M GWP.
- An MGA at 15-20% commission earns $60-80M a year of revenue.
- At MGA multiples of 10-15x revenue, that is a $0.6-1.2B valuation. Reaching $1B+ needs about 50% share of a market that does not exist yet.
- Software alone (200 funds × $150k) is about $30M ARR, which caps far below $1B.

**What pushes it past $1B:**
- extending to defence, space and advanced-manufacturing scale-up;
- taking balance-sheet risk as a carrier;
- becoming the rating standard that lenders require, a "Moody's for FOAK".

**Headwinds:** the 2025 OBBBA rescinded unobligated IRA LPO credit subsidy and the federal climate FOAK pipeline is shrinking. That is from memory, not re-verified here.

**Verdict:** a $1B outcome is possible, but it depends on a market that is currently roughly $100-300M of premium. That is close to the niche ceiling the founder already rejected.
deep.revolutionary_claim: It would create the first cross-technology loss history for novel hardware at scale-up. This is a reference-class base rate (probability of reaching X% of target by stage, slip distribution, which predecessor lineages predict success), assembled from about 30 years of government-forced project closeouts across DOE, ARPA-E, SBIR, Horizon and UKRI. Today every insurer and lender treats each FOAK as sui generis, priced by an independent engineer's opinion. If the base rates are predictive, technology risk becomes a priced, poolable peril, which is what climate project finance says is missing (per RFF, the barrier is that insurers lack historical data and risk-pooling).
deep.proof_idea:
One-day test of whether labels exist:
1. Pull the OSTI API metadata for about 500 FTRs from industry awardees (filter product type "Technical Report", sponsor EERE/ARPA-E, research org = company), in EERE classes like electrolyzers, biofuels/SAF, LDES and geothermal. The PDFs must be fetched off-container, or use OpenAlex S3 abstracts as a fallback.
2. Run an LLM extractor for (metric, target, achieved, unit, scale step, met/partially/not met, slip months, no-cost-extension) tuples.
3. Measure coverage: the share of FTRs that contain at least one quantitative target-versus-achieved pair. Kill threshold: below 30%.
4. Join awardees to outcomes: follow-on DOE awards, LPO commitments, SEC/press reports of plant COD, Chapter 11, and EIA-923 capacity factor via PUDL S3 for power assets.
5. Test whether "met goals" and lineage features predict follow-on success above a base rate (AUC).

The cheapest falsifier is step 3: if FTRs are mostly qualitative because the proprietary-exclusion rule strips numbers, the thesis dies.
deep.killers:
1) **The forcing rule cuts the wrong way.** EERE FTR guidance requires the goals-versus-accomplishments comparison but forbids proprietary or business-sensitive content, and allows up to 5-year protected-data embargoes. The exact quantitative performance numbers are the legally withholdable part. SBIR data rights now protect for 20 years. This is the opposite of SMAD, where raw data must be filed.

2. **Labels are sparse and badly censored.** Very few DOE-funded technologies reach a commercial FOAK. Lab or pilot results are a weak proxy for plant performance, because scale-up failures come from integration, feedstock and O&M, not the core metric. Plant-level outcomes are only observable for grid-connected assets (EIA-923). Underperformance at SAF, DAC, steel or chemicals plants is mostly private.

3. **Small, lumpy market with political dependency.** Today's technology performance insurance market is probably $100-300M of GWP. The US federal FOAK pipeline (LPO/IRA) was cut back in 2025. That puts this near the founder's rejected $100-200M niche.

4. **Incumbents have better data.** New Energy Risk, Munich Re and Ariel Green see full data rooms and independent-engineer reports on every deal they quote, which beats sanitised FTRs. Public R&D lineage would at best be a feature in their process.

5. **Being an MGA needs capacity.** Reinsurers will not hand pen to a model with no loss history. Years of policy seasoning are needed before credibility, which is a poor fit for the YC timeline. Adverse selection is also likely: the projects that seek a wrap are the riskier ones.

6. **Data reachability.** The core corpus (OSTI PDFs, CORDIS, GtR) is not mirrored on S3/GCS/GitHub, so the proof container cannot reach it without building a mirror.

7. **Not the founder's edge.** Insurance and actuarial credibility, plus carrier relationships, matter more than ML.

deep.name: Component-failure hazard engine for vehicle service contracts (UK MOT + Dutch APK defect panels)
deep.legal_basis_verified: Partly verified. DVSA still publishes the anonymised MOT bulk data under the Open Government Licence v3.0. open.data.dvsa.gov.uk/mot-anonymised has separate results and test-item (defect) zip files for 2022-2025. The 2025 files and a revised 2024 set were added on 22 June 2026, and data.gov.uk/CKAN holds the older years back to 2005. So key unknown 5 is resolved: bulk defect-item data has survived the move to the new API. The duty to test comes from the Road Traffic Act 1988 s.45-47; that is from memory, but it is uncontroversial. RDW 'Open Data RDW: Geconstateerde Gebreken' (APK defects per plate) is listed on data.overheid.nl. Its CC0 licence was not re-checked. One caveat matters for the thesis: what DVSA publishes is a byproduct of its own administrative system, not a disclosure of private claims data. It shows defects found at the test, not repairs or costs.
deep.data_access: MOT: annual ZIP/CSV pairs (test_result with test_id, vehicle_id, date, class, make, model, colour, fuel, cc, first_use_date, odometer, result; plus test_item with test_id, rfr_id and type: advisory, fail, PRS or dangerous) and an rfr lookup table. That is about 40M tests a year and tens of GB uncompressed across 2005-2025. It is OGL v3, so commercial use is allowed. The anonymised vehicle_id is meant to link a vehicle across years, which makes a longitudinal panel possible; confirm this is still true in the 2022+ files. Per-registration history needs the MOT History API, which requires registration plus an API key and is not for bulk use. RDW: Socrata endpoints on opendata.rdw.nl (APK defects, vehicle registry, odometer judgement), with no key needed. Reachability from the proof container: both open.data.dvsa.gov.uk and opendata.rdw.nl were tested and the proxy rejects them (CONNECT 403). I know of no official mirror on AWS Open Data, BigQuery public datasets, Zenodo or PyPI. GitHub search was blocked in this session. Kaggle and HF have partial community copies, but neither host is reachable either. A proof would need someone to download the data outside the container and push it to a GCS or S3 bucket or a GitHub release; that is easy, and the licence allows it.

deep.product_and_wedge: The wedge is an API that turns make, model, engine and age/mileage into component-level failure hazards (brakes, suspension, corrosion, emissions or exhaust, tyres, EV-specific wear). The vehicle's own MOT advisory trajectory conditions the estimate, and the API is sold to UK used-car warranty providers and dealer groups for warranty pricing and for declining risks at sale. critic:
# Final judge: both rounds combined

None of the 19 deep-dived candidates clears the bar as pure software. Every analytics-only version tops out at roughly $10-150M in revenue. A $1B outcome needs the data edge used to take risk (underwrite, transfer or lend), so the ranking below favours ideas where the forced public data creates an underwriting edge that incumbents lack.

## 1) Combined top 10

| # | Idea | Verdict (one line) | $1B path |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **End-of-life liability underwriter** (Alberta AER + Petrinex, then Saskatchewan, BC and US states) | Best mix of a law-created dataset, outcome labels, timing, uncrowded space and founder fit. Main risk is that the catalysts are policy-dependent. | Start by selling the liability score. Then sell closure surety and security bonds as an MGA on Canadian surety capacity. Then price and take over end-of-life liabilities from producers. Official Alberta liability is C$36.6B; a leaked AER estimate put it at C$260B. |
| 2 | **CA GeoTracker pollution-liability pricing** | The data is real (230M lab results) and contamination is an uninsured or badly priced peril. ## 2) Single best pick: end-of-life (closure) liability underwriter

Start with Alberta and Saskatchewan oil and gas wells and facilities, then extend to mine reclamation and solar/wind decommissioning.

**Quirk-created data edge**
- Alberta's licensing regime forces every licensee to file well licences and status changes, per-well production volumes, inspections and compliance records, and closure work.
- These are published as the AER ST37 well list and Petrinex public volumetrics.
- The Orphan Well Association (OWA) publishes the orphan inventory, which gives dated default labels with the former licensee named.
- Directive 088 forces mandatory closure spend, and Directive 011 sets the regulator's formula cost per well.
- So there are three things in public: a monthly panel of who holds which liability, outcome labels (which wells were orphaned), and the regulator's own deemed-cost formula to beat.
- This is the same pattern as SMAD: tenure law forces filings, and the public panel has never been modelled at well level for underwriting.
- Saskatchewan has its own licensee liability rating program and well data, a direct overlap with Dhruv's current work.

**Revolutionary ML**
- The official liability estimate is C$36.6B (C$23.4B inactive, C$13.2B active). The Auditor General said up to C$60B, and a leaked 2018 AER presentation said C$260B.
- That gap between C$36.6B and C$260B is the mispricing. Nobody has a per-well model of the true cost to close each well or the probability that it ends up orphaned.
- The AER itself still has no fixed approach to collecting security; decisions remain discretionary.
- Its June 2024 consultation proposes "performance and risk-informed security determination" and "alternative forms of security (bonds, trusts, etc)". The regulator is asking for exactly the model that does not exist yet.

**$1B path, in three layers**
- **(a) Liability score.** Sell it to sureties (for example Trisura and Intact, the natural first partners in Canadian surety), lenders and acquirers. Every licence transfer already triggers an AER security decision. Revenue is about $10-30M; this layer exists to win distribution and collect cost labels.
- **(b) Closure surety and security bonds as an MGA.** This opens once Alberta accepts bonds as security, and also covers Saskatchewan, BC, US state bonding and mine reclamation bonds.
  - Sizing: securing 10-20% of Alberta's C$36.6B at 1-3% rate on line is C$70-220M of premium a year in Alberta alone. This sizing is my estimate.
- **(c) Liability transfer, the largest pool.** Take inactive liabilities off producers for a cash fee priced by the model, then close them in batches below the fee.
  - Market size: C$23.4B of inactive liability in Alberta. US documented unplugged wells add plugging liability that independent estimates (RFF/EDF) put in the hundreds of billions (from memory).
  - Pace: industry already spends about C$900M a year on closure against a C$700M quota.
  - This is a balance-sheet business. The model is what keeps it from being the next R&Q-style mispricing failure.

**Uncrowded**
- My searches found no startup underwriting closure liability with ML; results were only academic, such as Insley (UWaterloo, 2024) on environmental bonds.
- Data vendors (XI Technologies' ARO tools, Enverus, geoLOGIC, from memory) sell estimates for acquisition analysis but take no risk and do not model probability of orphaning.

**Founder fit**
- Turning messy filings into predictions on geoscience records is exactly what Dhruv's team does: well files, casing and vent-flow reports, production histories.
- The opportunity is Canadian-first, with a Saskatchewan overlap to his current work. It is not a Terranox clone and finds no resources.

**Why it beats #2-#10**
- GeoTracker has a similar data edge, but LightBox owns its channel and its labels are biased.
- The PTAB and Korea ideas have stronger labels but an unstable regime or a licensing block.
- FOAK is more revolutionary but rests on a missing market.
- None of the others has a regulator actively designing a risk-based security regime that needs this model.

**Honest risks**
- **Brief-boundary risk.** It is resource-adjacent, but it is end-of-life liability, not prospecting or drilling.
- **The US catalyst is being reversed.** BLM's 2024 bonding rule (higher minimum bonds per lease and statewide) is being repealed by the current administration.
- **The Alberta catalyst is not yet in force.** AER's security framework is still undecided, and critics call the April 2025 Mature Asset Strategy reforms "smoke and mirrors".
- **Layer (c) needs a lot of capital.**
- **Capacity.** Sureties write against a model only once a carrier partner backs it.

## 3) One-day proof on real data

The question it answers: does a well-level model built from public filings predict orphaning materially better than the regulator's own Liability Management Rating (LMR)?

**Hour 0-1: stage the data outside the container.** The AER, Petrinex and OWA hosts are not github/pypi/s3/googleapis, and I found no mirror, so push the raw files to a GitHub release or GCS bucket.
- **AER ST37:** list of wells, current plus Wayback/archived monthly snapshots for 2015-2024. Gives licensee, status, fluid, depth, spud date and location.
- **Petrinex public conventional volumetric data:** monthly oil, gas and water volumes and days on, with operator ID, 2015-2025.
- **OWA orphan inventory:** wells and facilities with former licensee and designation date. Back it up with AER receivership and closure-order bulletins for dates.
- **Historical AER monthly LMR licensee ratings:** this is the baseline. Use archived copies.
- **Directive 011 cost tables:** the regulator's deemed cost per well.
- **AER surface casing vent flow / gas migration lists:** optional, if published.

**Hours 1-3: build the panel.**
- Build a well x month panel: holding licensee, status transitions, months since last production, decline, water cut, age, depth, H2S and region.
- Add licensee aggregates: the share of the licensee's liability that is inactive, the trend in its production revenue proxy, recent licence transfers, and its count of compliance hits.

**Hours 3-6: model.**
- Label: the well is in the OWA inventory, or its licensee was in receivership or under a closure order, within 48 months.
- Out-of-time design:
  - Train on 2015-2016 snapshots with outcomes through 2019.
  - Test on a December 2019 snapshot with outcomes 2020-2024. This window covers the 2020 receivership wave, so there are hundreds of licensees and thousands of wells in the labels.
- Model: LightBGM at well level, with licensee-level roll-up.
- Baselines:
  - the licensee's LMR ratio;
  - inactive share plus well age.

**Hours 6-8: metrics and cost check.**
- Metrics:
  - well-level and licensee-level AUC;
  - share of later-orphaned Directive 011 liability (dollars) captured in the top risk decile;
  - median lead time ahead of receivership.
- Cost side check: compare Directive 011 deemed cost with the OWA's reported actual closure costs, using annual-report averages by well type. Note that per-well actual costs are the gap a surety or area-based-closure partner would fill.

**Kill criteria.** Kill the idea if any of these hold:
- AUC lift over the LMR baseline is under 0.05;
- the top decile captures less than 50% of orphaned liability dollars;
- median lead time is under 6 months.

**Deliverable:** a ranked league table of current licensees by orphan risk. That is the artifact to put in front of Trisura or Intact surety underwriters and the AER's security-framework team.
